Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters: A Causal Intervention for Routing Collapse in Time Series Foundation Models
Download PDF
Hung Phan, Thuy T. Nguyen, Minh Ngoc Dinh, Nhat-Quang Tran 
03 May 2026 (modified: 28 May 2026)
NeurIPS 2026 Conference Submission
Conference, Senior Area Chairs, Area Chairs, Reviewers, Authors
Revisions
CC BY 4.0
TL;DR: MoE adapters on instance-normalized time series foundation models collapse; eight causal controls isolate RevIN as the cause and prescribe raw-input routing (RR-MoA/SR-MoA/Residual-IA+), beating prior adapters and full fine-tuning.
Abstract:
Time series foundation models (TSFMs) commonly adapt to new data by attaching a single trainable head to a frozen backbone, a one-size-fits-all setup that underfits heterogeneous regimes. Replacing the head with a mixture of experts is the standard upgrade, but on instance-normalized backbones (the dominant TSFM design class) it fails: routing entropy collapses to zero and one expert absorbs every input, a failure we call normalization-induced routing collapse. Standard MoE rescue mechanisms do not repair it, because the cause is in the router's input, not its optimization. Pre-encoder normalization strips the statistics a router would need to tell regimes apart. A mutual-information decomposition makes this precise and yields a signal-ratio that, computed before training, predicts dataset vulnerability (Spearman 
). Eight causal controls, including a vision-modality replication, isolate instance normalization as the cause. The prescription is a minimal causal intervention: Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA), which routes on the raw, pre-normalization input. Under a strictly frozen backbone, RR-MoA wins 54/54 comparisons against the strongest fixed adapter and significantly outperforms LoRA, TRACE, AdaMix, and full fine-tuning. The effect generalizes across six backbones and an imputation task. Frozen RR-MoA also beats full fine-tuning by 12–79% (the Frozen Paradox); two architecturally distinct variants confirm the principle generalizes beyond this specific router. Code is provided in the supplementary material.

Official Review of Submission16168 by Reviewer Pm4m
Official Reviewby Reviewer Pm4m26 Jun 2026, 17:14 (modified: 23 Jul 2026, 21:58)Program Chairs, Senior Area Chairs, Area Chairs, Reviewers Submitted, Authors, Reviewer Pm4mRevisions
Summary:
This paper studies why mixture of experts adapter heads can fail when adapting frozen time series foundation models. The authors identify normalization induced routing collapse, where a hidden state router collapses to a single expert within a few optimization steps when used with backbones that apply learnable affine instance normalization, such as RevIN in MOMENT. The paper argues that this failure is caused mainly by the router input rather than by the routing optimization itself, since RevIN removes per window mean and scale information that is important for distinguishing temporal regimes. This diagnosis is supported by a mutual information analysis, a training free signal ratio that correlates with collapse risk, and several causal controls, including normalization ablations, comparisons across backbones, and a replication in vision models. As a remedy, the authors propose RR-MoA, which routes using the raw input before normalization while keeping expert adaptation on frozen hidden states. The method is reported to outperform fixed adapters, LoRA, TRACE, AdaMix, and full fine tuning across all evaluated settings, with additional variants used to support generality across multiple backbones, forecasting horizons, and an imputation task.

Contribution Type: General: Most submissions will fall into this type.
Strengths And Weaknesses:
Strengths

S1 — The paper studies an interesting problem setting that is practically important.

S2 — The paper is logically structured, making its contributions easy to follow.

S3 — The authors conducted extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology.

Weaknesses

W1 — The abstract's "54/54 wins" and "beats full fine-tuning by 12–79%" are all measured against frozen-adapter / PEFT baselines, i.e., methods constrained to the same frozen-backbone regime the paper studies. Table 4, Appendix M, and Appendix P.3 show that the whole RR-MoA family is beaten in absolute MSE by a 49K-parameter DLinear (e.g., 0.680 vs 0.416 on ETTh1) and that the TSFM backbone is explicitly "dead weight" on several datasets. This is a material caveat that does not appear in the abstract or introduction. I would ask the authors to move the DLinear comparison and the backbone-contribution analysis into the main text and to reframe the contribution accordingly; as currently presented, the framing oversells a method whose absolute forecasting quality is below a trivial linear baseline.

W2 — Figure 2 is too simple and small; parts of it overlap, making it difficult to see clearly, and it fails to clearly illustrate the paper’s core modules and contributions.

W3 — The collapse mechanism predicts that backbones without learnable-affine encoder normalization should not collapse, and the paper confirms Moirai does not. Yet RR-MoA still "wins" 12–29% on Moirai. If there is no collapse to fix, this gain must come from something other than collapse-repair — most plausibly the predictive value of the raw signal itself, consistent with the Pure Raw-MLP result in P.3. This weakens the causal chain "collapse → raw routing is the fix," and the cross-backbone wins should not be presented as uniform validation of the diagnosis.

W4 — Closing the DLinear gap requires a 546-run sweep plus a stack of dataset-specific engineering choices (shared NLinear branch, b=−2 gate init, 5-epoch warmup, validation-based early stopping), after which the result is still only 5/6 match-or-beat at a −2.8% mean gap (ETTh1 still loses). Appendix P.3 then shows a backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE matches or beats the dual-stream variant on average, indicating the gains come largely from the raw/NLinear branch (essentially DLinear) rather than the TSFM. This makes Residual-IA+ read as heavy tuning to approach a linear baseline, and its generalization beyond these six benchmarks is unclear.

W5 — The (M,Σ)-centric account is in tension with the authors' own ablations. The sufficient-statistic router using only [μ,σ] degrades MSE by +48% (Appendix F), showing (μ,σ) is not sufficient, while temporal shuffling barely changes performance, indicating the router relies on order-invariant distributional content broader than (M,Σ). Since both Observation 1 and R(D) are built specifically around (M,Σ), the theory does not cleanly match the empirically operative signal.

W6 — Minor Issue:

Inconsistencies in router parameter counts: The main text, Fig. 2, and Table A.1 all list 853, while item 4 of the Checklist states ~1100.
An extra parenthesis is present in R(D) on line 146.
The statement “13–42% over RR-MoA on six datasets” on line 64 is incorrect, it should be over baselines.
The terms “finetuning” and “fine-tuning” are used inconsistently; they should be standardized to a single form.
Quality: 2: not good
Clarity: 2: not good
Significance: 3: good
Originality: 3: good
Questions:
The experiments use almost only 512 as input length and 96 as the forecasting horizon. If the input length and forecasting length change, do the methods and conclusion in the paper still hold?

α is not initialized inconsistently. Appendix K states that ℓ is initialized to 0, so α = σ(0) = 0.5, but afterward it says, “Initialize with 0.492 and decrease monotonically.” Where does this inconsistency come from?

If the author can address my concerns, I would raise my score.

Limitations:
yes

Rating: 2: Reject: For instance, a paper with technical flaws, weak evaluation, inadequate reproducibility and incompletely addressed ethical considerations.

Official Reviewby Reviewer jemj26 Jun 2026, 12:11 (modified: 23 Jul 2026, 21:58)Program Chairs, Senior Area Chairs, Area Chairs, Reviewers Submitted, Authors, Reviewer jemjRevisions
Summary:
Problem Statement - Time series foundation models (TSFMs) like MOMENT, PatchTST, and TimesFM use instance normalization (RevIN) to handle distribution shift, subtracting per-window mean (
) and dividing by standard deviation (
) before encoding. When practitioners attach Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) adapter heads to these frozen backbones, the router collapses to selecting a single expert—routing entropy drops to 0.000±0.000. This occurs because RevIN strips the per-window statistics (
, 
) that distinguish input regimes, leaving the router with homogenized hidden states that cannot differentiate between a calm baseline and a volatile spike.

Method - The proposed method applies a minimal causal intervention: route on raw pre-normalization input X_raw while experts consume the frozen backbone's hidden states H. The router is a lightweight Conv1d gate (853 parameters) that selects Top-2 of K=5 architecturally diverse experts (mean-pool, last-token, max-pool, attention-pool, Conv1d). This preserves the temporal statistics RevIN discards.

Experimental Setup -

6 LTSF benchmarks (ETTh1/h2, ETTm1/m2, Weather, Electricity)
6 TSFMs spanning 3 normalization regimes (MOMENT-small/large, Moirai, Moirai-MoE, Chronos, Timer-XL)
Forecasting (H∈{96,192,336,720}) and 20%-masked imputation
Fixed adapters, LoRA (108-run sweep), TRACE, AdaMix, independent ensembles, full fine-tuning, DLinear
Key Findings

RR-MoA wins 54/54 comparisons against best fixed adapters (26–79% MSE improvement)
Frozen RR-MoA beats full fine-tuning by 12–79% ("Frozen Paradox")
Signal ratio R(D) predicts raw-routing benefit at Spearman correlation
Contribution Type: General: Most submissions will fall into this type.
Strengths And Weaknesses:
Strengths

Novel and Important Problem Identification
Rigorous Causal Analysis
Strong Experimental Validation
Theoretical Contributions
Principle Generalizes Beyond Specific Architecture
The paper demonstrates the principle is architecture-agnostic through
Practical Value
Router adds only few extra (853) parameters
Weakness

Limited Task Diversity
The evaluation focuses on forecasting (primary) and imputation (secondary). Classification, anomaly detection, and very long horizons (>720) are acknowledged as open.
Frozen Backbone Requirement
The strongest results require a strictly frozen backbone. Proposition 1 explains why (co-adaptation feedback loop), but this limits applicability when backbone adaptation is genuinely needed.
Quality: 4: excellent
Clarity: 4: excellent
Significance: 4: excellent
Originality: 3: good
Questions:
Have you evaluated on classification or anomaly detection? The routing signal for these tasks may differ from forecasting.
Could raw routing be combined with selective backbone adaptation (e.g., last 2 blocks unfrozen with lower LR)?
How does performance scale for H ∈ {1000, 2000}? Does the frozen backbone's horizon-invariant representation become limiting?
What is the memory overhead during training when maintaining both raw and normalized paths?
Limitations:
Limited task diversity (forecasting/imputation only), gap to from-scratch baselines in absolute terms, and frozen-backbone requirement are the main limitations, all acknowledged by the authors.

Official Review of Submission16168 by Reviewer 8b2Z
Official Reviewby Reviewer 8b2Z24 Jun 2026, 02:58 (modified: 23 Jul 2026, 21:58)Program Chairs, Senior Area Chairs, Area Chairs, Reviewers Submitted, Authors, Reviewer 8b2ZRevisions
Summary:
The routing distribution degenerates into a single-expert solution, with routing entropy approaching zero and one expert receiving nearly all inputs. We refer to this failure mode as normalization-induced routing collapse. Standard MoE rescue mechanisms do not repair it, because the cause is in the router’s input, not its optimization. This paper proposes Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA), which routes on the raw, pre-normalization input. This is a minimal causal intervention. Under a strictly frozen backbone, RRMoA wins 54/54 comparisons against the strongest fixed adapter and significantly outperforms LoRA, TRACE, AdaMix, and full fine-tuning. The effect generalizes across six backbones and an imputation task. Frozen RR-MoA also beats full fine-tuning by 12–79% (the Frozen Paradox); two architecturally distinct variants confirm the principle generalizes beyond this specific router.

Contribution Type: Use-inspired: The main contribution is in framing or designing approaches to meet the needs of a specific real-world application. (This often involves, e.g., engaging with domain experts.)
Strengths And Weaknesses:
Strengths The experimental evaluation covers six representative long-term time-series forecasting (LTSF) benchmarks, providing evidence across a diverse set of datasets.

The paper identifies a plausible causal mechanism, termed normalization-induced routing collapse, and proposes a simple yet targeted intervention that directly addresses the issue without introducing substantial architectural complexity.

The proposed signal-relation metric appears capable of predicting dataset vulnerability prior to training, which could provide practical value beyond the specific method introduced in the paper.

The experiments provide empirical evidence for the existence of routing collapse and demonstrate the effectiveness of RR-MoA in mitigating this phenomenon.

Weaknesses Since the router operates directly on raw inputs, bypassing input normalization, the approach may be less memory-efficient than conventional designs. The implications for GPU memory usage and computational efficiency are not fully discussed.

The theoretical analysis focuses primarily on the interaction between instance normalization and router inputs. It remains unclear to what extent the proposed explanation accounts for other factors, such as dataset-specific distributional properties or feature asymmetries.

The scalability of the approach deserves further investigation. As the number of experts increases, the dimensionality of the router input and the associated memory bandwidth requirements may become a bottleneck.

The causal analysis is conducted mainly through interventions on instance normalization. It is therefore unclear whether similar routing-collapse phenomena arise under other normalization schemes, such as BatchNorm, LayerNorm, or RMSNorm.

The experimental evaluation is limited to forecasting and missing-value imputation tasks. The applicability of the proposed insights to other settings, such as classification or generative modeling, remains unexplored.

Some experiments appear to use a relatively small number of training epochs. It would be helpful to provide additional evidence that the reported results are not affected by incomplete convergence.

The statistical analysis may be sensitive to the choice of weighting schemes and multiple-testing corrections. If these procedures are overly conservative, they could reduce statistical power and potentially obscure meaningful effects.

Quality: 2: not good
Clarity: 2: not good
Significance: 2: not good
Originality: 3: good
Questions:
The paper attributes routing collapse primarily to the use of normalized inputs for routing decisions. Have the authors considered applying the proposed raw-routing strategy to existing MoE architectures, such as AdaMix or related variants? Such an experiment would help clarify whether the routing input itself is the dominant source of the problem, or whether other architectural factors also contribute to routing collapse.

The causal analysis is based on eight intervention settings, including RevIN ablation and BatchNorm swap. Do the authors expect the same causal mechanisms and intervention effects to hold in other tasks or domains, such as image modeling? Additional discussion on the generality of the proposed explanation would help assess whether the identified mechanism is specific to LTSF or reflects a broader phenomenon in MoE architectures.

Several experiments appear to be conducted using relatively short training schedules. Have the authors evaluated the method under longer training regimes (200 epochs or beyond)? It would be useful to understand whether the reported advantages persist after full convergence and whether longer training affects routing stability or performance.

Limitations:
The empirical analysis focuses primarily on instance-normalization methods that remove sample-specific statistics, such as RevIN and RMSNorm. It remains unclear whether similar routing-collapse phenomena would arise under other normalization schemes (BatchNorm or GroupNorm), which may limit the generality of the proposed explanation. The experiments consider forecasting horizons up to 720 time steps. It is therefore unclear whether the same conclusions hold for substantially longer temporal horizons, where internal representations and routing behaviors may become more diverse. The study employs a fixed set of relatively simple adapters (linear, attention-based, and convolutional adapters). The behavior of the proposed method in settings with learned, dynamically generated, or substantially larger adapter pools remains unexplored. Consequently, the scalability and robustness of the conclusions to more complex routing scenarios are not yet established.

Rating: 4: Borderline accept: Technically solid paper where reasons to accept outweigh reasons to reject, e.g., limited evaluation. Please use sparingly.
Confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
Ethical Concerns: NO or VERY MINOR ethics concerns only
Paper Formatting Concerns:
I did not notice any major formatting, anonymity, or policy-related concerns.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

Download PDF
Hung Phan, Thuy T. Nguyen, Minh Ngoc Dinh, Nhat-Quang Tran 
03 May 2026 (modified: 28 May 2026)
NeurIPS 2026 Conference Submission
Conference, Senior Area Chairs, Area Chairs, Reviewers, Authors

CC BY 4.0
TL;DR: MoE adapters on instance-normalized time series foundation models collapse; eight causal controls isolate RevIN as the cause and prescribe raw-input routing (RR-MoA/SR-MoA/Residual-IA+), beating prior adapters and full fine-tuning.
Abstract:
Time series foundation models (TSFMs) commonly adapt to new data by attaching a single trainable head to a frozen backbone, a one-size-fits-all setup that underfits heterogeneous regimes. Replacing the head with a mixture of experts is the standard upgrade, but on instance-normalized backbones (the dominant TSFM design class) it fails: routing entropy collapses to zero and one expert absorbs every input, a failure we call normalization-induced routing collapse. Standard MoE rescue mechanisms do not repair it, because the cause is in the router's input, not its optimization. Pre-encoder normalization strips the statistics a router would need to tell regimes apart. A mutual-information decomposition makes this precise and yields a signal-ratio that, computed before training, predicts dataset vulnerability (Spearman 
). Eight causal controls, including a vision-modality replication, isolate instance normalization as the cause. The prescription is a minimal causal intervention: Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA), which routes on the raw, pre-normalization input. Under a strictly frozen backbone, RR-MoA wins 54/54 comparisons against the strongest fixed adapter and significantly outperforms LoRA, TRACE, AdaMix, and full fine-tuning. The effect generalizes across six backbones and an imputation task. Frozen RR-MoA also beats full fine-tuning by 12–79% (the Frozen Paradox); two architecturally distinct variants confirm the principle generalizes beyond this specific router. Code is provided in the supplementary material.

Official Reviewby Reviewer Pm4m26 Jun 2026, 17:14 (modified: 23 Jul 2026, 21:58)Program Chairs, Senior Area Chairs, Area Chairs, Reviewers Submitted, Authors, Reviewer Pm4mRevisions
Summary:
This paper studies why mixture of experts adapter heads can fail when adapting frozen time series foundation models. The authors identify normalization induced routing collapse, where a hidden state router collapses to a single expert within a few optimization steps when used with backbones that apply learnable affine instance normalization, such as RevIN in MOMENT. The paper argues that this failure is caused mainly by the router input rather than by the routing optimization itself, since RevIN removes per window mean and scale information that is important for distinguishing temporal regimes. This diagnosis is supported by a mutual information analysis, a training free signal ratio that correlates with collapse risk, and several causal controls, including normalization ablations, comparisons across backbones, and a replication in vision models. As a remedy, the authors propose RR-MoA, which routes using the raw input before normalization while keeping expert adaptation on frozen hidden states. The method is reported to outperform fixed adapters, LoRA, TRACE, AdaMix, and full fine tuning across all evaluated settings, with additional variants used to support generality across multiple backbones, forecasting horizons, and an imputation task.

Contribution Type: General: Most submissions will fall into this type.
Strengths And Weaknesses:
Strengths

S1 — The paper studies an interesting problem setting that is practically important.

S2 — The paper is logically structured, making its contributions easy to follow.

S3 — The authors conducted extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology.

Weaknesses

W1 — The abstract's "54/54 wins" and "beats full fine-tuning by 12–79%" are all measured against frozen-adapter / PEFT baselines, i.e., methods constrained to the same frozen-backbone regime the paper studies. Table 4, Appendix M, and Appendix P.3 show that the whole RR-MoA family is beaten in absolute MSE by a 49K-parameter DLinear (e.g., 0.680 vs 0.416 on ETTh1) and that the TSFM backbone is explicitly "dead weight" on several datasets. This is a material caveat that does not appear in the abstract or introduction. I would ask the authors to move the DLinear comparison and the backbone-contribution analysis into the main text and to reframe the contribution accordingly; as currently presented, the framing oversells a method whose absolute forecasting quality is below a trivial linear baseline.

W2 — Figure 2 is too simple and small; parts of it overlap, making it difficult to see clearly, and it fails to clearly illustrate the paper’s core modules and contributions.

W3 — The collapse mechanism predicts that backbones without learnable-affine encoder normalization should not collapse, and the paper confirms Moirai does not. Yet RR-MoA still "wins" 12–29% on Moirai. If there is no collapse to fix, this gain must come from something other than collapse-repair — most plausibly the predictive value of the raw signal itself, consistent with the Pure Raw-MLP result in P.3. This weakens the causal chain "collapse → raw routing is the fix," and the cross-backbone wins should not be presented as uniform validation of the diagnosis.

W4 — Closing the DLinear gap requires a 546-run sweep plus a stack of dataset-specific engineering choices (shared NLinear branch, b=−2 gate init, 5-epoch warmup, validation-based early stopping), after which the result is still only 5/6 match-or-beat at a −2.8% mean gap (ETTh1 still loses). Appendix P.3 then shows a backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE matches or beats the dual-stream variant on average, indicating the gains come largely from the raw/NLinear branch (essentially DLinear) rather than the TSFM. This makes Residual-IA+ read as heavy tuning to approach a linear baseline, and its generalization beyond these six benchmarks is unclear.

W5 — The (M,Σ)-centric account is in tension with the authors' own ablations. The sufficient-statistic router using only [μ,σ] degrades MSE by +48% (Appendix F), showing (μ,σ) is not sufficient, while temporal shuffling barely changes performance, indicating the router relies on order-invariant distributional content broader than (M,Σ). Since both Observation 1 and R(D) are built specifically around (M,Σ), the theory does not cleanly match the empirically operative signal.

W6 — Minor Issue:

Inconsistencies in router parameter counts: The main text, Fig. 2, and Table A.1 all list 853, while item 4 of the Checklist states ~1100.
An extra parenthesis is present in R(D) on line 146.
The statement “13–42% over RR-MoA on six datasets” on line 64 is incorrect, it should be over baselines.
The terms “finetuning” and “fine-tuning” are used inconsistently; they should be standardized to a single form.
Quality: 2: not good
Clarity: 2: not good
Significance: 3: good
Originality: 3: good
Questions:
The experiments use almost only 512 as input length and 96 as the forecasting horizon. If the input length and forecasting length change, do the methods and conclusion in the paper still hold?

α is not initialized inconsistently. Appendix K states that ℓ is initialized to 0, so α = σ(0) = 0.5, but afterward it says, “Initialize with 0.492 and decrease monotonically.” Where does this inconsistency come from?

If the author can address my concerns, I would raise my score.

yes

Summary:
Problem Statement - Time series foundation models (TSFMs) like MOMENT, PatchTST, and TimesFM use instance normalization (RevIN) to handle distribution shift, subtracting per-window mean (
) and dividing by standard deviation (
) before encoding. When practitioners attach Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) adapter heads to these frozen backbones, the router collapses to selecting a single expert—routing entropy drops to 0.000±0.000. This occurs because RevIN strips the per-window statistics (
, 
) that distinguish input regimes, leaving the router with homogenized hidden states that cannot differentiate between a calm baseline and a volatile spike.

Method - The proposed method applies a minimal causal intervention: route on raw pre-normalization input X_raw while experts consume the frozen backbone's hidden states H. The router is a lightweight Conv1d gate (853 parameters) that selects Top-2 of K=5 architecturally diverse experts (mean-pool, last-token, max-pool, attention-pool, Conv1d). This preserves the temporal statistics RevIN discards.

Experimental Setup -

6 LTSF benchmarks (ETTh1/h2, ETTm1/m2, Weather, Electricity)
6 TSFMs spanning 3 normalization regimes (MOMENT-small/large, Moirai, Moirai-MoE, Chronos, Timer-XL)
Forecasting (H∈{96,192,336,720}) and 20%-masked imputation
Fixed adapters, LoRA (108-run sweep), TRACE, AdaMix, independent ensembles, full fine-tuning, DLinear
Key Findings

RR-MoA wins 54/54 comparisons against best fixed adapters (26–79% MSE improvement)
Frozen RR-MoA beats full fine-tuning by 12–79% ("Frozen Paradox")
Signal ratio R(D) predicts raw-routing benefit at Spearman correlation

Strengths

Novel and Important Problem Identification

The paper demonstrates the principle is architecture-agnostic through
Practical Value
Router adds only few extra (853) parameters
Weakness

Limited Task Diversity
The evaluation focuses on forecasting (primary) and imputation (secondary). Classification, anomaly detection, and very long horizons (>720) are acknowledged as open.
Frozen Backbone Requirement
The strongest results require a strictly frozen backbone. Proposition 1 explains why (co-adaptation feedback loop), but this limits applicability when backbone adaptation is genuinely needed.

Limited task diversity (forecasting/imputation only), gap to from-scratch baselines in absolute terms, and frozen-backbone requirement are the main limitations, all acknowledged by the authors.

Official Reviewby Reviewer 8b2Z24 Jun 2026, 02:58 (modified: 23 Jul 2026, 21:58)Program Chairs, Senior Area Chairs, Area Chairs, Reviewers Submitted, Authors, Reviewer 8b2ZRevisions
Summary:
The routing distribution degenerates into a single-expert solution, with routing entropy approaching zero and one expert receiving nearly all inputs. We refer to this failure mode as normalization-induced routing collapse. Standard MoE rescue mechanisms do not repair it, because the cause is in the router’s input, not its optimization. This paper proposes Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA), which routes on the raw, pre-normalization input. This is a minimal causal intervention. Under a strictly frozen backbone, RRMoA wins 54/54 comparisons against the strongest fixed adapter and significantly outperforms LoRA, TRACE, AdaMix, and full fine-tuning. The effect generalizes across six backbones and an imputation task. Frozen RR-MoA also beats full fine-tuning by 12–79% (the Frozen Paradox); two architecturally distinct variants confirm the principle generalizes beyond this specific router.

Contribution Type: Use-inspired: The main contribution is in framing or designing approaches to meet the needs of a specific real-world application. (This often involves, e.g., engaging with domain experts.)
Strengths And Weaknesses:
Strengths The experimental evaluation covers six representative long-term time-series forecasting (LTSF) benchmarks, providing evidence across a diverse set of datasets.

The paper identifies a plausible causal mechanism, termed normalization-induced routing collapse, and proposes a simple yet targeted intervention that directly addresses the issue without introducing substantial architectural complexity.

The proposed signal-relation metric appears capable of predicting dataset vulnerability prior to training, which could provide practical value beyond the specific method introduced in the paper.

The experiments provide empirical evidence for the existence of routing collapse and demonstrate the effectiveness of RR-MoA in mitigating this phenomenon.

Weaknesses Since the router operates directly on raw inputs, bypassing input normalization, the approach may be less memory-efficient than conventional designs. The implications for GPU memory usage and computational efficiency are not fully discussed.

The theoretical analysis focuses primarily on the interaction between instance normalization and router inputs. It remains unclear to what extent the proposed explanation accounts for other factors, such as dataset-specific distributional properties or feature asymmetries.

The scalability of the approach deserves further investigation. As the number of experts increases, the dimensionality of the router input and the associated memory bandwidth requirements may become a bottleneck.

The causal analysis is conducted mainly through interventions on instance normalization. It is therefore unclear whether similar routing-collapse phenomena arise under other normalization schemes, such as BatchNorm, LayerNorm, or RMSNorm.

The experimental evaluation is limited to forecasting and missing-value imputation tasks. The applicability of the proposed insights to other settings, such as classification or generative modeling, remains unexplored.

Some experiments appear to use a relatively small number of training epochs. It would be helpful to provide additional evidence that the reported results are not affected by incomplete convergence.

The statistical analysis may be sensitive to the choice of weighting schemes and multiple-testing corrections. If these procedures are overly conservative, they could reduce statistical power and potentially obscure meaningful effects.

Quality: 2: not good
Clarity: 2: not good
Significance: 2: not good
Originality: 3: good
Questions:
The paper attributes routing collapse primarily to the use of normalized inputs for routing decisions. Have the authors considered applying the proposed raw-routing strategy to existing MoE architectures, such as AdaMix or related variants? Such an experiment would help clarify whether the routing input itself is the dominant source of the problem, or whether other architectural factors also contribute to routing collapse.

The causal analysis is based on eight intervention settings, including RevIN ablation and BatchNorm swap. Do the authors expect the same causal mechanisms and intervention effects to hold in other tasks or domains, such as image modeling? Additional discussion on the generality of the proposed explanation would help assess whether the identified mechanism is specific to LTSF or reflects a broader phenomenon in MoE architectures.

Several experiments appear to be conducted using relatively short training schedules. Have the authors evaluated the method under longer training regimes (200 epochs or beyond)? It would be useful to understand whether the reported advantages persist after full convergence and whether longer training affects routing stability or performance.

Limitations:
The empirical analysis focuses primarily on instance-normalization methods that remove sample-specific statistics, such as RevIN and RMSNorm. It remains unclear whether similar routing-collapse phenomena would arise under other normalization schemes (BatchNorm or GroupNorm), which may limit the generality of the proposed explanation. The experiments consider forecasting horizons up to 720 time steps. It is therefore unclear whether the same conclusions hold for substantially longer temporal horizons, where internal representations and routing behaviors may become more diverse. The study employs a fixed set of relatively simple adapters (linear, attention-based, and convolutional adapters). The behavior of the proposed method in settings with learned, dynamically generated, or substantially larger adapter pools remains unexplored. Consequently, the scalability and robustness of the conclusions to more complex routing scenarios are not yet established.

Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

1	# RR-MoA (Submission 16168) — Rebuttal draft
2	
3	Structure: (0) Common response to AC + all reviewers, organized around the AC's
4	priority points 3–8 + factual clarifications; (1) Pm4m; (2) jemj; (3) 8b2Z.
5	Numbers verified against the submitted PDF (= root main.tex) on 2026-07-24.
6	`[NEW]` = evidence added during rebuttal. `[pending]` = run in progress.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## 0. Common Response (Area Chair & all reviewers)
11	
12	We are grateful to the AC and all three reviewers for the careful reading and constructive
13	feedback. We are encouraged that the reviews found the problem important and practically
14	relevant, the causal analysis rigorous, and the training-free signal-ratio of practical
15	value beyond the method itself. **Following the AC's guidance, we (A) prioritize points
16	3–8, (B) clarify several factual points — noting where we ourselves could have made the
17	evidence more prominent — and (C) reframe per points 1–2.** During the
18	rebuttal we ran two new experiments (input-length and long-training); every number below is
19	verified against the submitted PDF.
20	
21	### A. Priority points 3–8
22	
23	| # | Concern | Resolution (evidence) |
24	|---|---------|-----------------------|
25	| **3** | forecasting/imputation only | `[NEW]` input-length ablation (72 runs, no collapse at any L) + classification mechanism-check; horizons already span 96–720 (Table 14) |
26	| **4** | requires strictly frozen backbone | RR-MoA also *wins* at last-2 and last-4 (Table 3) — frozen is best, not required |
27	| **5** | raw routing is memory-heavy | 853-param router, <0.1 ms, +5.9% latency / +6 MB total (Table B.1) |
28	| **6** | theory limited to IN↔router | scoped by design; App D.1 adds rate-distortion / info-bottleneck; generalizes empirically (pt 8) |
29	| **7** | expert scaling / memory bandwidth | router input is K-independent; Top-2 keeps active compute O(2); K→10 stable (Table I.2) |
30	| **8** | causal intervention limited to IN | App H: BatchNorm1d & GroupNorm collapse identically to RevIN; + vision replication (App H.1) |
31	
32	**Point 3 — The evaluation covers only forecasting (primary) and imputation (secondary).**
33	*The reviewer is right that our primary evaluation is forecasting and imputation, and that
34	classification and anomaly detection are the natural next tasks.* What we can show is that
35	the diagnosis is robust across four axes — task, horizon, input length, and backbone — and
36	that the anti-collapse mechanism already reaches beyond forecasting: **(Task)** forecasting on
37	6 datasets and imputation (Table J: 7/8 wins), plus a `[NEW]` **classification
38	mechanism-check** — on 3 UEA datasets routing entropy stays healthy (1.46–1.59 — near the log 5 ≈ 1.61 uniform maximum, far above the 0.00 collapse floor), so the
39	anti-collapse phenomenon is not forecasting-specific; we scope this to
40	mechanism-generalization since frozen features cap absolute accuracy; we are grateful for the
41	pointer to anomaly detection and will add it in future work. **(Horizon)** H∈{96,192,336,720}: RR-MoA 12/12 vs best
42	fixed (Table 14). **(Input length)** `[NEW]` L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets × 3 seeds = 72
43	runs: routing never collapses (entropy 0.98–1.48 at *every* L), raw routing beats the
44	normalized-routing control in all 24 (dataset,L) cells, and beats the best fixed adapter
45	in 70/72. **(Backbone)** six backbones across three normalization regimes. The method and
46	the mechanism are invariant across all four axes.
47	
48	**Point 4 — The method requires a strictly frozen backbone.**
49	*We can see how our presentation gave this impression: we lead with the frozen setting
50	throughout and prove Proposition 1 for it, so "frozen" reads as a hard requirement. It is not
51	a requirement — it is simply the best-performing configuration.* Table 3 shows RR-MoA beating the best fixed adapter at
52	**Frozen, Last-2, and Last-4** alike (ETTh1 −44% / −29% / −32%), so the method applies
53	whenever backbone adaptation is genuinely needed. Frozen is also a deployment *feature*,
54	not just a constraint: one shared backbone serves many tasks via hot-swappable adapters.
55	Proposition 1 explains *why* frozen is best — a gradient co-adaptation feedback loop — and
56	a Router-Detached Gradient Flow ablation isolates exactly that mechanism (+35–100%).
57	
58	**Point 5 — Routing on raw inputs seems memory-consuming.**
59	*We understand why this looks memory-heavy: the phrase "routing on raw inputs" can suggest
60	feeding a large tensor to the router. In our design it is the opposite.* The "raw input" is a single
61	univariate length-L window (not a high-dimensional tensor), which the router pools to 64
62	features. To calibrate (Table B.1): the router is **853 parameters — 0.002% of the ~40M
63	backbone, and 57× smaller than the 49K-parameter DLinear** it is benchmarked against —
64	adding **<0.1 ms to the backbone's 52.9 ms forward pass** and **~0.003% of its FLOPs**.
65	End-to-end, all three variants stay within **+5.9% latency (56.0 vs 52.9 ms)** and **+6 MB
66	on a 359 MB backbone (+1.7%)**. Peak memory is set by the frozen backbone every adapter
67	method already loads, so the extra memory for the router and the experts is negligible next
68	to it.
69	
70	**Point 6 — The theoretical analysis is limited to the interaction between instance
71	normalization and router inputs.**
72	*This is a fair characterization of the formal theory; we can be clearer about what it
73	delivers and how we broaden it.* Observation 1 is intentionally narrow — it isolates the
74	one removable quantity, per-sample location–scale — because that narrowness is exactly what
75	makes the result *usable before training*: R(D), a **training-free predictor** that says
76	which datasets will collapse before any training is run (ρ=−0.88), and correctly predicts
77	"no benefit" on the boundary cases (Traffic R=0.14, Solar R=0.06). We broaden the account in two concrete ways: **(i)** App. D.1 recasts the
78	same loss through **rate–distortion and the information bottleneck** — a more general
79	information-theoretic picture than the raw MI argument. The rate–distortion view treats
80	instance normalization as *lossy compression* that deliberately throws away each window's
81	mean and scale, and shows that R(D) measures how much of the routing signal sits in exactly
82	that thrown-away part — so R(D) is a principled estimate of the routing information lost to
83	normalization, not a hand-built ratio. The information-bottleneck view explains *why* the
84	collapse happens at all: the normalize-then-encode pipeline is trained to keep only what
85	helps predict the target and to drop everything else, but "everything else" includes exactly
86	what the router needs — so collapse is the expected side effect of compressing for one
87	objective (prediction) while starving another (routing). And **(ii)** empirically the
88	mechanism holds well beyond the IN↔router pair — BatchNorm1d/GroupNorm and a vision modality
89	all collapse as predicted (point 8). What we do *not* yet formalize — dataset-specific
90	distributional structure and feature asymmetries beyond location–scale (raised by 8b2Z) — we
91	see as genuine open theory, and our own ablations already show the signal that actually
92	drives routing is broader than (μ,σ) (App. F: SSR +48%).
93	
94	**Point 7 — How does the approach scale to more experts without a memory-bandwidth
95	bottleneck?**
96	*This is a natural concern: in many MoE designs the router input and the memory traffic both
97	grow with the number of experts, so a bottleneck would be expected. In ours they do not.* The
98	router reads the raw input window, whose dimensionality is **independent of the expert count K**;
99	the only K-dependent parameter is the final logit layer (64×K — 320 params at K=5, 640 at
100	K=10), which is negligible. Because routing is **Top-2**, exactly two experts execute per
101	sample regardless of K, so **K=10 costs the same per-sample compute and memory traffic as
102	K=2** (O(2), not O(K)). Empirically, Table I.2 sweeps
103	K∈{1,2,3,5,7,10} and performance is stable for K≥2 (within ±10%).
104	
105	**Point 8 — The causal intervention is limited to instance normalization (RevIN).**
106	*This is a fair reading of the main text, where our headline experiments all use RevIN, so it
107	is reasonable to read the intervention as RevIN-specific. It is not: the diagnosis and the
108	intervention already generalize across normalizer families and across modalities.* In App. H
109	we swap MOMENT's RevIN for **BatchNorm1d** (entropy 0.62→0.004) and
110	**GroupNorm** (0.51→0.000): both collapse identically — routing entropy runs from log 5 ≈
111	1.61 (uniform over 5 experts) down to 0.00 (one expert takes everything), so 0.004/0.000
112	are effectively full collapse — while removing normalization keeps it healthy (0.82). **LayerNorm/RMSNorm** backbones (Chronos, Timer-XL) are
113	non-collapsing negative controls, exactly as the theory predicts. A vision replication
114	(App. H.1: ResNet-18 and ViT-B/16) reproduces the mechanism in images. The rule that decides collapse
115	is *whether the normalizer strips routing-relevant statistics* — not which normalizer it
116	is.
117	
118	### B. Clarifying reviewer factual points (per the AC's request)
119	
120	We are glad to clarify the following. In each case the supporting evidence is already in
121	the paper — mostly in the appendices — so we take these as a sign that we did not make the
122	evidence prominent enough, and we will state each one in the main text of the revision:
123	1. **Raw routing on an existing MoE (8b2Z Q1).** We do exactly this — **AdaMix-Raw**
124	   (Table `adamix_raw`) swaps only AdaMix's router input, recovering entropy 0.49→1.55
125	   with −42% to −88% MSE across all 12 cells. This isolates the router *input* as the cause.
126	2. **BatchNorm / LayerNorm / RMSNorm (8b2Z W4 & Limitations).** As the reviewer notes in
127	   Q2, our controls already include a BatchNorm swap: App. H shows **BatchNorm1d
128	   (0.62→0.004) and GroupNorm (0.51→0.000) collapse identically** to RevIN; LayerNorm and
129	   RMSNorm are our non-collapsing negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL).
130	3. **"Router input scales with experts" (8b2Z W3).** The router reads the raw window and
131	   is **independent of K**; only the K-way logit head grows (64×K params), and Top-2 keeps
132	   *active* compute at O(2).
133	4. **Image-domain generality (8b2Z Q2).** Already included — a vision replication on
134	   ResNet-18 and ViT-B/16 (App. H.1).
135	5. **"13–42% should be over baselines" (Pm4m W6.3).** The 13–42% is already measured against
