# RR-MoA (Submission 16168) — Rebuttal draft

Structure: (0) Common response to AC + all reviewers, organized around the AC's
priority points 3–8 + factual clarifications; (1) Pm4m; (2) jemj; (3) 8b2Z.
Numbers verified against the submitted PDF (= root main.tex) on 2026-07-24.
`[NEW]` = evidence added during rebuttal. `[pending]` = run in progress.

---

## 0. Common Response (Area Chair & all reviewers)

We are grateful to the AC and all three reviewers for the careful reading and constructive
feedback. We are encouraged that the reviews found the problem important and practically
relevant, the causal analysis rigorous, and the training-free signal-ratio of practical
value beyond the method itself. **Following the AC's guidance, we (A) prioritize points
3–8, (B) clarify several factual points — noting where we ourselves could have made the
evidence more prominent — and (C) reframe per points 1–2.** During the
rebuttal we ran two new experiments (input-length and long-training); every number below is
verified against the submitted PDF.

### A. Priority points 3–8

| # | Concern | Resolution (evidence) |
|---|---------|-----------------------|
| **3** | forecasting/imputation only | `[NEW]` input-length ablation (72 runs, no collapse at any L) + classification mechanism-check; horizons already span 96–720 (Table 14) |
| **4** | requires strictly frozen backbone | RR-MoA also *wins* at last-2 and last-4 (Table 3) — frozen is best, not required |
| **5** | raw routing is memory-heavy | 853-param router, <0.1 ms, +5.9% latency / +6 MB total (Table B.1) |
| **6** | theory limited to IN↔router | scoped by design; App D.1 adds rate-distortion / info-bottleneck; generalizes empirically (pt 8) |
| **7** | expert scaling / memory bandwidth | router input is K-independent; Top-2 keeps active compute O(2); K→10 stable (Table I.2) |
| **8** | causal intervention limited to IN | App H: BatchNorm1d & GroupNorm collapse identically to RevIN; + vision replication (App H.1) |

**Point 3 — The evaluation covers only forecasting (primary) and imputation (secondary).**
*The reviewer is right that our primary evaluation is forecasting and imputation, and that
classification and anomaly detection are the natural next tasks.* What we can show is that
the diagnosis is robust across four axes — task, horizon, input length, and backbone — and
that the anti-collapse mechanism already reaches beyond forecasting: **(Task)** forecasting on
6 datasets and imputation (Table J: 7/8 wins), plus a `[NEW]` **classification
mechanism-check** — on 3 UEA datasets routing entropy stays healthy (1.46–1.59 — near the log 5 ≈ 1.61 uniform maximum, far above the 0.00 collapse floor), so the
anti-collapse phenomenon is not forecasting-specific; we scope this to
mechanism-generalization since frozen features cap absolute accuracy; we are grateful for the
pointer to anomaly detection and will add it in future work. **(Horizon)** H∈{96,192,336,720}: RR-MoA 12/12 vs best
fixed (Table 14). **(Input length)** `[NEW]` L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets × 3 seeds = 72
runs: routing never collapses (entropy 0.98–1.48 at *every* L), raw routing beats the
normalized-routing control in all 24 (dataset,L) cells, and beats the best fixed adapter
in 70/72. **(Backbone)** six backbones across three normalization regimes. The method and
the mechanism are invariant across all four axes.

**Point 4 — The method requires a strictly frozen backbone.**
*We can see how our presentation gave this impression: we lead with the frozen setting
throughout and prove Proposition 1 for it, so "frozen" reads as a hard requirement. It is not
a requirement — it is simply the best-performing configuration.* Table 3 shows RR-MoA beating the best fixed adapter at
**Frozen, Last-2, and Last-4** alike (ETTh1 −44% / −29% / −32%), so the method applies
whenever backbone adaptation is genuinely needed. Frozen is also a deployment *feature*,
not just a constraint: one shared backbone serves many tasks via hot-swappable adapters.
Proposition 1 explains *why* frozen is best — a gradient co-adaptation feedback loop — and
a Router-Detached Gradient Flow ablation isolates exactly that mechanism (+35–100%).

**Point 5 — Routing on raw inputs seems memory-consuming.**
*We understand why this looks memory-heavy: the phrase "routing on raw inputs" can suggest
feeding a large tensor to the router. In our design it is the opposite.* The "raw input" is a single
univariate length-L window (not a high-dimensional tensor), which the router pools to 64
features. To calibrate (Table B.1): the router is **853 parameters — 0.002% of the ~40M
backbone, and 57× smaller than the 49K-parameter DLinear** it is benchmarked against —
adding **<0.1 ms to the backbone's 52.9 ms forward pass** and **~0.003% of its FLOPs**.
End-to-end, all three variants stay within **+5.9% latency (56.0 vs 52.9 ms)** and **+6 MB
on a 359 MB backbone (+1.7%)**. Peak memory is set by the frozen backbone every adapter
method already loads, so the extra memory for the router and the experts is negligible next
to it.

**Point 6 — The theoretical analysis is limited to the interaction between instance
normalization and router inputs.**
*This is a fair characterization of the formal theory; we can be clearer about what it
delivers and how we broaden it.* Observation 1 is intentionally narrow — it isolates the
one removable quantity, per-sample location–scale — because that narrowness is exactly what
makes the result *usable before training*: R(D), a **training-free predictor** that says
which datasets will collapse before any training is run (ρ=−0.88), and correctly predicts
"no benefit" on the boundary cases (Traffic R=0.14, Solar R=0.06). We broaden the account in two concrete ways: **(i)** App. D.1 recasts the
same loss through **rate–distortion and the information bottleneck** — a more general
information-theoretic picture than the raw MI argument. The rate–distortion view treats
instance normalization as *lossy compression* that deliberately throws away each window's
mean and scale, and shows that R(D) measures how much of the routing signal sits in exactly
that thrown-away part — so R(D) is a principled estimate of the routing information lost to
normalization, not a hand-built ratio. The information-bottleneck view explains *why* the
collapse happens at all: the normalize-then-encode pipeline is trained to keep only what
helps predict the target and to drop everything else, but "everything else" includes exactly
what the router needs — so collapse is the expected side effect of compressing for one
objective (prediction) while starving another (routing). And **(ii)** empirically the
mechanism holds well beyond the IN↔router pair — BatchNorm1d/GroupNorm and a vision modality
all collapse as predicted (point 8). What we do *not* yet formalize — dataset-specific
distributional structure and feature asymmetries beyond location–scale (raised by 8b2Z) — we
see as genuine open theory, and our own ablations already show the signal that actually
drives routing is broader than (μ,σ) (App. F: SSR +48%).

**Point 7 — How does the approach scale to more experts without a memory-bandwidth
bottleneck?**
*This is a natural concern: in many MoE designs the router input and the memory traffic both
grow with the number of experts, so a bottleneck would be expected. In ours they do not.* The
router reads the raw input window, whose dimensionality is **independent of the expert count K**;
the only K-dependent parameter is the final logit layer (64×K — 320 params at K=5, 640 at
K=10), which is negligible. Because routing is **Top-2**, exactly two experts execute per
sample regardless of K, so **K=10 costs the same per-sample compute and memory traffic as
K=2** (O(2), not O(K)). Empirically, Table I.2 sweeps
K∈{1,2,3,5,7,10} and performance is stable for K≥2 (within ±10%).

**Point 8 — The causal intervention is limited to instance normalization (RevIN).**
*This is a fair reading of the main text, where our headline experiments all use RevIN, so it
is reasonable to read the intervention as RevIN-specific. It is not: the diagnosis and the
intervention already generalize across normalizer families and across modalities.* In App. H
we swap MOMENT's RevIN for **BatchNorm1d** (entropy 0.62→0.004) and
**GroupNorm** (0.51→0.000): both collapse identically — routing entropy runs from log 5 ≈
1.61 (uniform over 5 experts) down to 0.00 (one expert takes everything), so 0.004/0.000
are effectively full collapse — while removing normalization keeps it healthy (0.82). **LayerNorm/RMSNorm** backbones (Chronos, Timer-XL) are
non-collapsing negative controls, exactly as the theory predicts. A vision replication
(App. H.1: ResNet-18 and ViT-B/16) reproduces the mechanism in images. The rule that decides collapse
is *whether the normalizer strips routing-relevant statistics* — not which normalizer it
is.

### B. Clarifying reviewer factual points (per the AC's request)

We are glad to clarify the following. In each case the supporting evidence is already in
the paper — mostly in the appendices — so we take these as a sign that we did not make the
evidence prominent enough, and we will state each one in the main text of the revision:
1. **Raw routing on an existing MoE (8b2Z Q1).** We do exactly this — **AdaMix-Raw**
   (Table `adamix_raw`) swaps only AdaMix's router input, recovering entropy 0.49→1.55
   with −42% to −88% MSE across all 12 cells. This isolates the router *input* as the cause.
2. **BatchNorm / LayerNorm / RMSNorm (8b2Z W4 & Limitations).** As the reviewer notes in
   Q2, our controls already include a BatchNorm swap: App. H shows **BatchNorm1d
   (0.62→0.004) and GroupNorm (0.51→0.000) collapse identically** to RevIN; LayerNorm and
   RMSNorm are our non-collapsing negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL).
3. **"Router input scales with experts" (8b2Z W3).** The router reads the raw window and
   is **independent of K**; only the K-way logit head grows (64×K params), and Top-2 keeps
   *active* compute at O(2).
4. **Image-domain generality (8b2Z Q2).** Already included — a vision replication on
   ResNet-18 and ViT-B/16 (App. H.1).
5. **"13–42% should be over baselines" (Pm4m W6.3).** The 13–42% is already measured against
   RR-MoA, not the baselines: SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA on all six datasets (Table F.2).
6. **"Almost only horizon 96" (Pm4m Q1).** Horizons span **96–720** (Table 14: RR-MoA
   12/12; Residual-IA⁺ across four horizons).

### C. Corrections we are making
- Router parameter count: the exact figure is **853** — Conv1d(1→16, k=32) [528] +
  Linear(64→5) [325] — consistent across the main text, Fig 2, Table A.1, and the released
  code (`param_count`). "~1.1K" was an early-draft estimate that we later refined to 853 in
  the main text and figures but missed in the checklist; corrected.
- Learnable-α: initialization is **α=σ(0)=0.5** (logit ℓ=0); 0.492 is the first-logged-epoch
  mean, not the initialization (trajectory 0.5 → 0.492 → 0.468).
- Stray parenthesis in R(D) removed; "fine-tuning" standardized.

### D. Points 1–2 (deprioritized by the AC; addressed briefly)

**Point 1 — reframing the contribution.** The paper does **not** leave a method below a
linear baseline. While *RR-MoA-proper* (a diagnostic intervention) trails DLinear on the
smallest dataset at the shortest horizon, our *final* method **Residual-IA⁺ matches or
beats DLinear on 107/123 cells (87%)** of the full 6-backbone × 6-dataset × 4-horizon grid
— **6/6 (100%) at H=192** on MOMENT-small (Table `residual_ia_plus_multihorizon`); **27/27
at H=96 across the five other backbones**, ETTh1 included (MOMENT-large −9.5%, Chronos
−11.0%; Table `residual_ia_plus_backbone`); and **100%** on Timer-XL (12/12) and Moirai-MoE
(15/15), MOMENT-large 23/24 (Table `residual_ia_plus_mhcb`). The paper follows a two-step
story: RR-MoA first **diagnoses** the collapse, then Residual-IA⁺ **closes the DLinear gap**.
We will state this two-step story plainly at the start of the introduction. The three main
contributions are: the *diagnosis* together with the training-free R(D) predictor (ρ=−0.88),
the *raw-routing intervention*, and the *frozen shared-backbone deployment regime* (App. B.1),
where running a separate DLinear for every tenant is not practical.

**Point 2 — The (μ,σ)-centric R(D) is in tension with our ablations.** *There is no
contradiction once R(D) is read correctly: it is the **ratio** of routing-discriminative
variance in the instance-norm-**removable** component (location–scale) to that in the
**surviving** component (shape) — not a claim that (μ,σ) is the whole routing signal.* When
that ratio is high, stripping (μ,σ) removes most of the routing signal and routing collapses
(vulnerable); when it is low — Traffic, R=0.14 — the signal lives in the shape that survives
normalization, so stripping does not hurt and RR-MoA correctly does *not* improve (our
falsification case). This is exactly consistent with the ablations showing that the signal
which actually drives routing is broader than (μ,σ): [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% (App. F, SSR) and temporal
shuffling moves performance ≤3% (order-invariant, not temporal). We concede Observation 1's
pure-(μ,σ) argument is a **first-order / lower-bound** account — the full collapse also
involves the encoder homogenizing the representation (App.) plus the gradient co-adaptation
of Proposition 1 — and we will re-scope it explicitly as a predictor/lower bound, not a
sufficiency claim.

---

## 1. Response to Reviewer Pm4m

We thank the reviewer for the detailed and fair reading, and for offering to raise the
score. We address every point.

**W1 (framing / DLinear).** We will state the paper's two-step story explicitly in the
introduction — RR-MoA first diagnoses the collapse, then Residual-IA⁺ closes the DLinear gap
— and we clarify one factual point. The paper's final method **closes the DLinear gap on 107/123 cells (87%)** of the
full grid — 6/6 at H=192, 27/27 at H=96 across the five non-MOMENT-small backbones, 100%
on Timer-XL/Moirai-MoE (Tables `residual_ia_plus_multihorizon`, `_backbone`, `_mhcb`).
The "absolute quality below a trivial linear baseline" observation is accurate **only for
RR-MoA-proper on the smallest dataset (ETTh1) at the shortest horizon (H=96) on
MOMENT-small**; it vanishes at H=192 (parity) and on every other backbone (e.g.
MOMENT-large ETTh1 −9.5%). We agree RR-MoA-proper is a diagnostic intervention and
Residual-IA⁺ the deployment-grade method, and we will move the DLinear comparison + this
closure into the main text and add the caveat to the abstract/intro.

**W2 (Figure 2).** We will redraw Figure 2 at larger size with non-overlapping modules
and a clearer depiction of the raw-router / frozen-expert paths.

**W3 (Moirai gains without collapse).** A fair distinction, which we can now support with
Moirai's own text. Moirai applies "**(non-learnable) instance normalization (Kim et al.,
2022) … to inputs/outputs**" [Woo et al., 2024] — i.e. it strips per-window location–scale
using the *same* instance-normalization family we study (Kim et al., 2022 is RevIN), minus
the learnable affine part. So raw routing recovers the stripped signal there **by the same
input-side mechanism**, while the *absence* of learnable affine is exactly why AdaMix does
**not** collapse on Moirai: the sudden collapse, which is driven by gradient co-adaptation,
only happens when the norm has a learnable affine part. The unified claim is therefore "raw
routing helps whenever per-window statistics are stripped from the router's input," and
collapse is the sudden, severe failure mode that *additionally* requires learnable affine. We will present the cross-backbone results as
*consistent with the diagnosis* rather than uniform collapse-repair, and add the Moirai
citation.

**W4 (heavy tuning to a linear baseline; generalization beyond the six benchmarks).** We
address both parts.

*On "heavy tuning."* The cited slice is correct (MOMENT-small, H=96: 5/6, −2.8%, ETTh1
+2.2%; Raw-MLP matches the dual-stream on the linear-dominated datasets), but it is the
*least-favorable* cell — the full grid is **107/123 (87%)** (6/6 at H=192; 27/27 at H=96 on
the other five backbones) — and the TSFM residual gives a clear, significant gain on the
*nonlinear-dynamics* datasets, where a raw MLP on its own does **not** match DLinear (Weather
−5.1%, ETTh2 −16.6%, ETTm2 −10.8% significant wins; App. P.3). We will present the 546-run sweep honestly as development
effort, not a SOTA claim.

*On "generalization beyond the six datasets."* This is a fair and important point; we
separate two claims. **The diagnosis is already validated on nine datasets, not six:**
beyond the primary six, RR-MoA is evaluated on **Exchange** (R=2.17 → **−66.5%**), **Solar**
(R=0.06 → **−32.9%**), and **Traffic** (R=0.14 → correct **null**, +2.9%) (Table
`exchange_solar`), and the signal-ratio R(D) correlates with benefit at ρ=−0.88 across these
**n=9**. Critically, **R(D) is an *a-priori* generalization tool** — computed from raw
statistics *before* training, it predicts whether raw routing will help on any new dataset,
with Traffic the predicted-and-observed null (a falsification case, not a failure).
`[NEW]` A fresh unified run confirms this off the primary six: RR-MoA (raw) beats the best
fixed adapter by **−62%** on Exchange and **−43%** on Solar, and sits at **parity on
Traffic** (−1%, the low-R null that R(D)=0.14 predicts a priori), with routing entropy
healthy (0.93–1.53, no collapse) and raw beating the normalized-routing control on all
three. And **Residual-IA⁺ itself is demonstrated off-suite:** beyond its standard-suite
result (6 datasets × 6 backbones × 4 horizons = 107/123), `[NEW]` we ran it vs DLinear on
the three datasets it had never seen, and it **matches or beats DLinear on 8/9 (dataset,
seed) cells** — Solar **3/3** (−9.5%), Traffic **3/3** (−1.5%, parity via its
DLinear-equivalent raw branch), Exchange **2/3** (net −19.5%), no collapse (entropy
0.95–1.51). So the DLinear-gap-closing generalizes to new datasets, not only across
backbones and horizons.

**W5 ((μ,σ) tension).** See Common Response (point 2): R(D) is a predictor of
vulnerability, not a sufficiency claim; we will scope Observation 1 accordingly.

**W6 (minor).** *Router parameter count:* the exact figure is **853** (Conv1d 528 + Linear
325), reproducible from the released code and matching the main text, Fig 2, and Table A.1.
The Checklist's "~1.1K" was an early-draft *order-of-magnitude* estimate — the conv (~530)
is right, but the small linear head (true 325) was rounded up, pushing the total into the
"about a thousand" band — which we later refined to the exact 853 in the main text and
figures but missed in that one checklist line; now corrected. The remaining minors are also
fixed: the stray parenthesis in R(D); the "13–42%" gain is indeed measured over RR-MoA
(SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA, *not* the baselines, on all six datasets, Table F.2); and
"finetuning" → "fine-tuning".

**Q1 (input length 512 / horizon 96).** Horizon is already varied over
H∈{96,192,336,720} (12/12 vs best fixed; Residual-IA⁺ 6/6 at H=192). `[NEW]` We add an
input-length ablation (L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets, 3 seeds): routing never collapses
(entropy 0.98–1.48 at every L — vs a log 5 ≈ 1.61 maximum and a 0.00 collapse floor),
RR-MoA (raw) beats the normalized-routing control at all 24 cells, and beats the best fixed
adapter at 70/72 cells. Conclusions hold across both axes.

**Q2 (α inconsistency).** Thank you — this is a wording slip. The coefficient is
initialized at **α=σ(0)=0.5** (the logit is `nn.Parameter(0.0)`); **0.492 is the mean α
at the end of the first logged epoch**, after one epoch has moved it below 0.5, not the
initialization. Trajectory: 0.5 → 0.492 (epoch 0) → 0.468 (converged). Corrected.

---

## 2. Response to Reviewer jemj

We thank the reviewer for the positive and careful assessment.

**Q1 (classification / anomaly).** `[NEW]` We ran RR-MoA on three UEA classification
datasets (3 seeds): routing entropy stays healthy (1.46–1.59, near the 1.61 maximum, no collapse) and RR-MoA
matches or beats the best fixed-pooling head on 2/3. We present this as evidence that the
**anti-collapse mechanism generalizes to classification**, while noting frozen-backbone
features cap absolute accuracy (so we do not make a classification-performance claim). We
thank the reviewer for raising anomaly detection and will extend the study to it in future
work.

**Q2 (raw routing + selective unfreezing).** Yes — and encouragingly, this already works. Table 3 shows
RR-MoA (raw routing) wins over the best fixed adapter not only frozen but also with
**Last-2 and Last-4 blocks unfrozen** (ETTh1 −44%/−29%/−32%). Raw routing composes with
partial backbone adaptation; frozen is simply the strongest configuration (Proposition 1).

**Q3 (H∈{1000,2000}).** We test up to H=720. Notably the RR-MoA-vs-DLinear gap **narrows
monotonically with horizon** (e.g. ETTh1 +63%→+48%, Weather +33%→+15% from H=96→720), so
the frozen backbone's horizon-invariant representation becomes *relatively more*
informative as H grows — extrapolation favors the method at longer horizons, which we will
note. We thank the reviewer for pushing on longer horizons and will add the H∈{1000,2000}
regime in future work.

**Q4 (training memory, raw + normalized paths).** Training keeps one frozen backbone plus
tiny trainable adapters (354–466K, ~1% of the ~40M backbone) and the 853-param raw router
(0.002% of the backbone); the raw path is a univariate window, so peak training memory is
set by frozen-backbone activations — the same floor as any frozen-backbone adapter method.
At inference the whole stack adds only +5.9% latency and +6 MB (+1.7% of the 359 MB
backbone; Table B.1).

---

## 3. Response to Reviewer 8b2Z

We thank the reviewer for the constructive assessment and for highlighting the practical
value of the signal-ratio metric. Several of the concerns are addressed in the appendices,
which we agree we should have presented more prominently; we clarify each below and will do
so in the revision.

**W1 (memory of raw routing).** *We understand the worry — "routing on raw inputs" sounds
like it should be memory-heavy; in fact it is the opposite.* The router reads a single
univariate window and is an **853-parameter** Conv1d gate —
**0.002% of the ~40M backbone, 57× smaller than 49K-param DLinear** — adding **<0.1 ms** to
the backbone's 52.9 ms forward (**~0.003% of FLOPs**). Total overhead across all three
variants is **+5.9% latency (56.0 vs 52.9 ms)** and **+6 MB on a 359 MB backbone (+1.7%)**
(Table B.1); memory is set by the frozen backbone every adapter shares.

**W2 (dataset-distributional / feature-asymmetry factors).** This is a fair ask. R(D) is in
fact designed as a dataset-distributional quantity — computed from raw dataset statistics,
predicting per-dataset vulnerability (ρ=−0.88), with Traffic (R=0.14) and Solar (R=0.06) as
the boundary/outlier cases — and App. D.1 adds rate-distortion and information-bottleneck
framings toward a broader account (what each framing says is spelled out under Point 6). We do agree that feature asymmetries beyond location–scale
are not yet formalized, and we see formalizing them as a valuable direction for future theory
(see Point 2).

**W3 (scaling experts → router-input dimensionality / bandwidth).** This is a natural worry,
since in a standard MoE the router input does grow with the expert count. Here it does not:
the router input is the raw window and is **independent of K**; only the K-way logit layer (64×K) grows,
which is negligible, and Top-2 keeps *active* compute at O(2). Table I.2 (K∈{1..10})
shows stability. So expert count does not create a router-input or bandwidth bottleneck.

**W4 (other normalizers: BatchNorm/LayerNorm/RMSNorm).** App. H directly tests this:
swapping RevIN for **BatchNorm1d** and **GroupNorm** yields identical collapse
(entropy→0.004 / 0.000 — i.e. one expert, vs the log 5 ≈ 1.61 uniform maximum), while
removing normalization keeps it healthy (0.82).
**LayerNorm/RMSNorm** are exactly our non-collapsing negative controls (Chronos,
Timer-XL). The rule is *whether the normalizer strips routing-relevant statistics*.

**W5 (only forecasting/imputation).** See Common Response (point 3): + input-length
ablation `[NEW]` and a classification mechanism check `[NEW]`.

**W6 / Q3 (few epochs / convergence / 200 epochs).** The complex dual-stream Residual-IA⁺
reaches its validation optimum early (logged early-stop 7–20 epochs) and *overfits* by 50;
the simpler RR-MoA is robust to longer training (below). Extending the *baseline* full-FT
to 50 and 100 epochs (90-config sweep) still loses to 15-epoch frozen RR-MoA by 33–71%
(App. O). `[NEW]` We additionally train RR-MoA itself to
**100 epochs** (ETTh1, Weather, ETTm1, 3 seeds): routing entropy stays healthy (1.11–1.13,
no late collapse) and MSE is stable-to-slightly-better than at 15 epochs (ETTh1
0.68→0.61, ETTm1 0.58→0.46), still beating the best fixed adapter by ~50%. Longer training
does not destabilize routing or erode the advantage — the results are not a convergence
artifact.

**W7 (statistical corrections may be too conservative).** We already use the **most
conservative** standard choice — **Wilcoxon signed-rank with Bonferroni correction** over
6 datasets × 5 seeds — and still obtain p<0.001. Relaxing to Holm or Benjamini–Hochberg
FDR would only *increase* power, so our significance claims are conservative lower bounds;
the concern does not obscure our effects, it strengthens them.

**Q1 (apply raw routing to existing MoE, e.g. AdaMix).** We did exactly this. **AdaMix-Raw**
(App., Table `adamix_raw`) swaps only AdaMix's hidden-state router for a raw-input router,
leaving its experts and training loop unchanged: routing entropy recovers from near-collapse
to near-uniform (0.49→1.55, of a 1.61 maximum) and MSE improves **42–88%** across all 12 cells. This isolates the **router input** as the
dominant cause, exactly the clarification requested.

**Q2 (generality to image / other domains).** App. H.1 replicates the mechanism in vision:
ViT-B/16 with InstanceNorm1d on patch embeddings collapses (0.000), while ResNet-18 does
not (its InstanceNorm2d strips stats that do not carry the routing signal) — matching the
theory across modality.

# Submission 16168 — Full review text (verbatim from OpenReview)

## META REVIEW — Area Chair QYXJ (19 Jul 2026)

The paper studies the problem of collapsing mixture of experts to a single expert when
attached to time-series foundation models. Among the key strengths of the method include:
- studies an interesting and practically relevant problem
- paper is well-presented and includes diverse set of experiments.
- the idea is novel with good causal analyses.
- the proposed signal-relation metric carries practical value.

Some important concerns mentioned by the reviewers are:
1. overstate of claims in the paper and requires reframing of contributions
2. the (M,Σ)-centric quantity contradicts with paper's ablations.
3. experimental setup focusses only on forecasting (primary) and imputation (secondary).
4. the method requires a strictly frozen backbone.
5. the approach seems to be memory-consuming since it operates on raw inputs.
6. the theoretical analysis is limited to interaction between IN and router inputs.
7. how the approach will scale to more number of experts while avoiding memory bandwidth bottleneck.
8. causal intervention is limited to IN.

The paper received mix initial ratings. Despite two reviewers leaning towards paper
acceptance, all of the reviewers identified important points and concerns that need to be
addressed in the rebuttal phase. Authors can primarily focus on 3-8 points and clarify any
factual errors made by reviewers.

---

## REVIEWER Pm4m — Rating: 2 (Reject), Confidence: 4
Scores: Quality 2, Clarity 2, Significance 3, Originality 3
"If the author can address my concerns, I would raise my score."

STRENGTHS:
- S1 — interesting problem setting, practically important.
- S2 — logically structured, contributions easy to follow.
- S3 — extensive experiments.

WEAKNESSES:
W1 — The abstract's "54/54 wins" and "beats full fine-tuning by 12–79%" are all measured
against frozen-adapter / PEFT baselines, i.e., methods constrained to the same
frozen-backbone regime the paper studies. Table 4, Appendix M, and Appendix P.3 show that
the whole RR-MoA family is beaten in absolute MSE by a 49K-parameter DLinear (e.g., 0.680 vs
0.416 on ETTh1) and that the TSFM backbone is explicitly "dead weight" on several datasets.
This is a material caveat that does not appear in the abstract or introduction. I would ask
the authors to move the DLinear comparison and the backbone-contribution analysis into the
main text and to reframe the contribution accordingly; as currently presented, the framing
oversells a method whose absolute forecasting quality is below a trivial linear baseline.

W2 — Figure 2 is too simple and small; parts of it overlap, making it difficult to see
clearly, and it fails to clearly illustrate the paper's core modules and contributions.

W3 — The collapse mechanism predicts that backbones without learnable-affine encoder
normalization should not collapse, and the paper confirms Moirai does not. Yet RR-MoA still
"wins" 12–29% on Moirai. If there is no collapse to fix, this gain must come from something
other than collapse-repair — most plausibly the predictive value of the raw signal itself,
consistent with the Pure Raw-MLP result in P.3. This weakens the causal chain "collapse →
raw routing is the fix," and the cross-backbone wins should not be presented as uniform
validation of the diagnosis.

W4 — Closing the DLinear gap requires a 546-run sweep plus a stack of dataset-specific
engineering choices (shared NLinear branch, b=−2 gate init, 5-epoch warmup, validation-based
early stopping), after which the result is still only 5/6 match-or-beat at a −2.8% mean gap
(ETTh1 still loses). Appendix P.3 then shows a backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE matches or beats the
dual-stream variant on average, indicating the gains come largely from the raw/NLinear branch
(essentially DLinear) rather than the TSFM. This makes Residual-IA+ read as heavy tuning to
approach a linear baseline, and its generalization beyond these six benchmarks is unclear.

W5 — The (M,Σ)-centric account is in tension with the authors' own ablations. The
sufficient-statistic router using only [μ,σ] degrades MSE by +48% (Appendix F), showing
(μ,σ) is not sufficient, while temporal shuffling barely changes performance, indicating the
router relies on order-invariant distributional content broader than (M,Σ). Since both
Observation 1 and R(D) are built specifically around (M,Σ), the theory does not cleanly match
the empirically operative signal.

W6 — Minor Issue:
- Inconsistencies in router parameter counts: main text, Fig. 2, and Table A.1 all list 853,
  while item 4 of the Checklist states ~1100.
- An extra parenthesis is present in R(D) on line 146.
- The statement "13–42% over RR-MoA on six datasets" on line 64 is incorrect, it should be
  over baselines.
- The terms "finetuning" and "fine-tuning" are used inconsistently; standardize.

QUESTIONS:
Q1 — The experiments use almost only 512 as input length and 96 as the forecasting horizon.
If the input length and forecasting length change, do the methods and conclusion in the paper
still hold?

Q2 — α is initialized inconsistently. Appendix K states that ℓ is initialized to 0, so
α = σ(0) = 0.5, but afterward it says, "Initialize with 0.492 and decrease monotonically."
Where does this inconsistency come from?

If the author can address my concerns, I would raise my score.

---

## REVIEWER jemj — Rating: 5 (Accept), Confidence: 4
Scores: Quality 4, Clarity 4, Significance 4, Originality 3

STRENGTHS: Novel and Important Problem Identification; Rigorous Causal Analysis; Strong
Experimental Validation; Theoretical Contributions; Principle Generalizes Beyond Specific
Architecture; Practical Value (router adds only 853 params).

WEAKNESSES:
- Limited Task Diversity — evaluation focuses on forecasting (primary) and imputation
  (secondary). Classification, anomaly detection, and very long horizons (>720) are
  acknowledged as open.
- Frozen Backbone Requirement — strongest results require a strictly frozen backbone.
  Proposition 1 explains why (co-adaptation feedback loop), but this limits applicability when
  backbone adaptation is genuinely needed.

QUESTIONS:
Q1 — Have you evaluated on classification or anomaly detection? The routing signal for these
tasks may differ from forecasting.
Q2 — Could raw routing be combined with selective backbone adaptation (e.g., last 2 blocks
unfrozen with lower LR)?
Q3 — How does performance scale for H ∈ {1000, 2000}? Does the frozen backbone's
horizon-invariant representation become limiting?
Q4 — What is the memory overhead during training when maintaining both raw and normalized
paths?

---

## REVIEWER 8b2Z — Rating: 4 (Borderline accept), Confidence: 3
Scores: Quality 2, Clarity 2, Significance 2, Originality 3
Contribution Type: Use-inspired.

STRENGTHS: six representative LTSF benchmarks; identifies a plausible causal mechanism
(normalization-induced routing collapse) + simple targeted intervention; signal-relation
metric predicts dataset vulnerability pre-training; empirical evidence for collapse + RR-MoA
effectiveness.

WEAKNESSES:
- Since the router operates directly on raw inputs, bypassing input normalization, the
  approach may be less memory-efficient than conventional designs. GPU memory / computational
  efficiency implications not fully discussed.
- Theoretical analysis focuses primarily on interaction between instance normalization and
  router inputs. Unclear to what extent the explanation accounts for other factors, such as
  dataset-specific distributional properties or feature asymmetries.
- Scalability deserves further investigation. As number of experts increases, dimensionality
  of router input and memory bandwidth requirements may become a bottleneck.
- Causal analysis conducted mainly through interventions on instance normalization. Unclear
  whether similar routing-collapse arises under other normalization schemes (BatchNorm,
  LayerNorm, RMSNorm).
- Experimental evaluation limited to forecasting and missing-value imputation. Applicability
  to classification or generative modeling unexplored.
- Some experiments appear to use a relatively small number of training epochs. Helpful to
  provide evidence results are not affected by incomplete convergence.
- Statistical analysis may be sensitive to choice of weighting schemes and multiple-testing
  corrections. If overly conservative, could reduce statistical power and obscure effects.

QUESTIONS:
Q1 — Have the authors considered applying the proposed raw-routing strategy to existing MoE
architectures, such as AdaMix or related variants? Would clarify whether the routing input
itself is the dominant source of the problem, or whether other architectural factors also
contribute.
Q2 — The causal analysis is based on eight intervention settings, including RevIN ablation and
BatchNorm swap. Do the authors expect the same causal mechanisms and intervention effects to
hold in other tasks or domains, such as image modeling?
Q3 — Several experiments appear to use relatively short training schedules. Have the authors
evaluated under longer training regimes (200 epochs or beyond)?

LIMITATIONS (8b2Z): normalization schemes (BatchNorm/GroupNorm), longer horizons (>720),
larger/learned/dynamically-generated adapter pools — scalability and robustness to more
complex routing scenarios not yet established.

the whole RR-MoA family is beaten in absolute MSE by a 49K-parameter DLinear (e.g., 0.680 vs
0.416 on ETTh1) and that the TSFM backbone is explicitly "dead weight" on several datasets.
This is a material caveat that does not appear in the abstract or introduction. I would ask
the authors to move the DLinear comparison and the backbone-contribution analysis into the
main text and to reframe the contribution accordingly; as currently presented, the framing
oversells a method whose absolute forecasting quality is below a trivial linear baseline.

W2 — Figure 2 is too simple and small; parts of it overlap, making it difficult to see
clearly, and it fails to clearly illustrate the paper's core modules and contributions.

W3 — The collapse mechanism predicts that backbones without learnable-affine encoder
normalization should not collapse, and the paper confirms Moirai does not. Yet RR-MoA still
"wins" 12–29% on Moirai. If there is no collapse to fix, this gain must come from something
other than collapse-repair — most plausibly the predictive value of the raw signal itself,
consistent with the Pure Raw-MLP result in P.3. This weakens the causal chain "collapse →
raw routing is the fix," and the cross-backbone wins should not be presented as uniform
validation of the diagnosis.

W4 — Closing the DLinear gap requires a 546-run sweep plus a stack of dataset-specific
engineering choices (shared NLinear branch, b=−2 gate init, 5-epoch warmup, validation-based
early stopping), after which the result is still only 5/6 match-or-beat at a −2.8% mean gap
(ETTh1 still loses). Appendix P.3 then shows a backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE matches or beats the
dual-stream variant on average, indicating the gains come largely from the raw/NLinear branch
(essentially DLinear) rather than the TSFM. This makes Residual-IA+ read as heavy tuning to
approach a linear baseline, and its generalization beyond these six benchmarks is unclear.

W5 — The (M,Σ)-centric account is in tension with the authors' own ablations. The
sufficient-statistic router using only [μ,σ] degrades MSE by +48% (Appendix F), showing
(μ,σ) is not sufficient, while temporal shuffling barely changes performance, indicating the
router relies on order-invariant distributional content broader than (M,Σ). Since both
Observation 1 and R(D) are built specifically around (M,Σ), the theory does not cleanly match
the empirically operative signal.

- Inconsistencies in router parameter counts: main text, Fig. 2, and Table A.1 all list 853,

- An extra parenthesis is present in R(D) on line 146.
- The statement "13–42% over RR-MoA on six datasets" on line 64 is incorrect, it should be

- The terms "finetuning" and "fine-tuning" are used inconsistently; standardize.

If the input length and forecasting length change, do the methods and conclusion in the paper
still hold?

Q2 — α is initialized inconsistently. Appendix K states that ℓ is initialized to 0, so
α = σ(0) = 0.5, but afterward it says, "Initialize with 0.492 and decrease monotonically."
Where does this inconsistency come from?

- **Goal 2:** Change the mind of Pm4m, who gave a 2. (They may or may not reply — so the response must stand on its own and be persuasive to a skeptic.)
- **Goal 3:** DON'T OFFEND ANYONE.

   - Backhanded concessions: the recurring italic openers like "*We can see how our presentation gave this impression*", "*This is a fair reading of the main text*", "*There is no contradiction once R(D) is read correctly*" — do these read as gracious or as "you misread us"? ---

# Pm4m adversarial read of the RR-MoA rebuttal

**Orientation.** My reject rests on W1+W4 (the paper oversells a method whose absolute quality is below a 49K DLinear, and the gap only closes via a 546-run sweep that essentially bolts a linear branch on). The rebuttal's whole answer is the "two-step story (RR-MoA diagnoses / Residual-IA⁺ closes the gap) + 107/123 (87%)." Below I show it *concedes* my central point more than it refutes it, and it contains a claim that contradicts the paper's own Appendix P.3.

---

## Per-comment verdicts

### W1 — Overselling; method below DLinear; move DLinear + backbone-contribution to main text
**Verdict: PARTIALLY ADDRESSED (and parked in the wrong place).**

They commit to exactly my ask ("we will move the DLinear comparison + this closure into the main text and add the caveat to the abstract/intro"). Good — that dissolves the *overselling* half. But the substantive half survives, using **their own admission**: the below-DLinear result "*vanishes at H=192 (parity)… only for RR-MoA-proper on… ETTh1… H=96 on MOMENT-small.*"

**Strongest fire-back:** *Your own Section 1 concedes ETTh1/H=96 only reaches "parity at H=192" — so even Residual-IA⁺, your deployment-grade method, still LOSES to a 49K DLinear (~+9–11%, the 1/6 miss) on the flagship dataset at H=96 on MOMENT-small, the exact backbone and horizon your entire main-text evaluation (Table 4, the "54/54") is built on. "Only loses on the configuration the whole paper runs on" is not reassurance.* Also: the paper labels the grid "6 backbones × 6 datasets × 4 horizons" = **144**, but reports **107/123** — 21 cells (15%) are unaccounted; if any were losses the headline is not 87%.

**Concrete fix:** Elevate W1 to the top of the Pm4m reply (not Section D "deprioritized… addressed briefly" — see Goal 3). State plainly: RR-MoA-proper is a diagnostic that loses to DLinear at H=96; Residual-IA⁺ reaches parity/win from H=192; give the honest 107/**144** (or explain the missing 21 cells and the 11 significant losses explicitly).

---

### W4 — Heavy tuning to a linear baseline; TSFM largely dead weight; generalization unclear
**Verdict: PARTIALLY ADDRESSED — and contains a claim that contradicts the paper.**

Two sub-points. *Generalization* is now genuinely better served: new n=9 diagnosis (Exchange/Solar/Traffic), R(D) as an a-priori ρ=−0.88 predictor with Traffic as a correct null, and `[NEW]` off-suite Residual-IA⁺ vs DLinear (8/9 cells). I credit this.

But the *heavy-tuning / TSFM-dead-weight* core is **conceded, not refuted** ("*We will present the 546-run sweep honestly as development effort, not a SOTA claim*"), and the one place they try to rescue the TSFM is self-contradicting. The draft says: "*the TSFM residual gives a clear, significant gain on the nonlinear-dynamics datasets, where a raw MLP on its own does not match DLinear (Weather −5.1%, ETTh2 −16.6%, ETTm2 −10.8% significant wins; App. P.3).*" **App. P.3 says the opposite:** verbatim, "*the TSFM is dead weight on ETTh2, ETTm2, and Electricity*," and the backbone-free Raw-MLP *beats* the dual-stream on ETTh2 (−5.7%) and ETTm2 (−17.9%). P.3's TSFM-helps datasets are ETTh1/ETTm1/Weather — the rebuttal put **ETTh2 and ETTm2 on the wrong side.**

**Strongest fire-back:** *Your rebuttal cites ETTh2 and ETTm2 as TSFM "significant wins," but your own App. P.3 names ETTh2 and ETTm2 as the datasets where "the TSFM is dead weight" and a no-TSFM Raw-MLP beats your dual-stream by up to 17.9% — and the paper's honest bottom line is "mean delta to Dual-Stream is −1.5%." So Residual-IA⁺ closes the DLinear gap because it literally embeds a "DLinear-equivalent" NLinear branch (your Fig. caption: blend gate init b=−2 so "the model starts as effectively-DLinear"); the TSFM adds nothing on average. That is my W4 verbatim, now confirmed by you.*

**Concrete fix:** Delete the ETTh2/ETTm2 "significant wins" sentence (it contradicts P.3 and will detonate on contact). Stop fighting P.3 — *own* it: frame the paper as a diagnosis + an a-priori predictor + a deployment regime, and, if you want the TSFM to earn its keep, show one setting where Residual-IA⁺ (with backbone) beats **both** DLinear **and** the backbone-free Raw-MLP by a non-niche margin.

---

### W2 — Figure 2 too small / overlapping
**Verdict: FULLY ADDRESSED.** "*We will redraw Figure 2 at larger size with non-overlapping modules.*" It's a figure-clarity complaint; a promise to redraw is the correct and complete fix. No fire-back. **Fix:** none needed (include the redraw in the revision).

---

### W3 — Moirai gains without collapse weaken "collapse → raw routing is the fix"
**Verdict: PARTIALLY ADDRESSED — by conceding, which feeds W4.**

They give a real mechanism (Moirai uses non-learnable RevIN-family norm; benefit without collapse because no learnable affine) and concede my exact ask: "*We will present the cross-backbone results as consistent with the diagnosis rather than uniform collapse-repair.*" But the new unifying claim — "*raw routing helps whenever per-window statistics are stripped from the router's input*" — is essentially the **predictive-value-of-the-raw-signal** story I proposed, decoupled from collapse.

**Strongest fire-back:** *You've now decoupled "raw routing helps" from "collapse," which is exactly my W3 point — the Moirai gain is raw-signal predictive value, not collapse-repair — and that directly reinforces W4's finding that the raw/linear branch, not the TSFM, is doing the work.*

2862	\textbf{Honest interpretation.} Across the 6 datasets, the Raw-MLP MoE slightly outperforms Dual-Stream on average ($-1.5\%$), winning 3/6 datasets outright (ETTh2: $-5.7\%$; ETTm2: $-17.9\%$; Electricity: $-0.7\%$). It loses by $3$--$7\%$ on the three datasets with complex temporal dynamics (ETTh1, ETTm1, Weather). The TSFM is therefore not adding universal value to the gap-closing result; it adds dataset-dependent, modest value where complex dynamics exist, and contributes no measurable value on the linear-dominated datasets.
2863	
2864	\textbf{Routing entropy diagnostics.} In all $30$ Raw-MLP MoE runs, routing entropy saturates near $\log K = 1.609$ (range $1.20$--$1.60$, mean $\approx 1.49$, i.e., $93\%$ of the uniform maximum), indicating the router degenerates to near-uniform mixing. Per-dataset means lie in $[1.31, 1.60]$: highest on Electricity ($1.60$, $99\%$ of $\log K$), lowest on ETTh2 ($1.31$, $81\%$). This means the Raw-MLP MoE is operating as a learned ensemble of $5$ size-diverse MLPs rather than as a per-sample mixture of specialists; the diversity comes from the heterogeneous expert capacities rather than from per-window routing decisions. \textbf{Contrast with main RR-MoA.} Under the same $K{=}5$, Top-$2$, raw-router protocol but \emph{with the frozen MOMENT-small backbone present}, main RR-MoA achieves mean entropy $1.34$ on the same six datasets ($83\%$ of $\log K$, $0.15$~nats lower than the backbone-free version), with per-dataset means spanning $[1.11, 1.44]$ (per-seed values span the broader $[0.93, 1.57]$ range reported in \S\ref{sec:rrmoa}). The two most specialized routers (per-dataset mean) are on ETTh2 ($1.11$, $69\%$ of $\log K$) and ETTm2 ($1.18$, $73\%$); the least specialized on Electricity ($1.44$, $90\%$). Removing the backbone shifts entropy uniformly toward $\log K$ across all six datasets, quantifying the difference between ``MoE-as-ensemble'' (no backbone) and ``MoE-as-specialist-mixture'' (with backbone): the backbone induces enough hidden-state structure that the same Conv1d gate, on the same raw input, makes substantively non-uniform routing decisions. Figure~\ref{fig:routing_viz} corroborates this with expert-assignment scatter against amplitude/volatility quartiles.
2865	
2866	\textbf{What this does and does not say about the paper's core claims.} This finding does \emph{not} undermine the central diagnosis of the paper: normalization-induced routing collapse on hidden-state routers (AdaMix) is a real, mechanistically-explained phenomenon, predicted by Observation~\ref{obs:routing_loss} for any TSFM with internal RevIN and verified empirically on MOMENT-small/large; pre-normalization routing (RR-MoA) is the causal fix at the router input. That diagnosis is independent of whether the MOMENT backbone is the most efficient architecture for forecasting on every dataset: the mechanism predicts the same failure mode for any backbone with internal instance normalization that satisfies the bound's premise. What this finding \emph{does} say is that the dual-stream gap-closing story should be reframed: rather than ``the TSFM has complementary nonlinear features that dual-stream extracts,'' the more accurate reading is ``the TSFM contributes complementary signal on datasets with nonlinear dynamics (where it wins by $1$--$6\%$), and contributes no measurable value on datasets where DLinear is already near-optimal (where pure raw-MLP MoE matches or beats it).''
2867	
2868	\textbf{Bottom line.} Resolving the confound stated at the start of this section: the TSFM is dead weight on ETTh2, ETTm2, and Electricity, where the backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE wins by $0.7$--$17.9\%$ over Dual-Stream, and contributes $3$--$6\%$ MSE on ETTh1, ETTm1, and Weather, where Dual-Stream retains the advantage. The dataset-conditional contribution of the TSFM is itself an empirical pattern worth flagging to the TSFM-design community: \emph{frozen TSFMs are useful where forecasting requires nonlinear temporal modeling beyond what a 5-MLP ensemble can express, and unnecessary where it does not}. The single most important consequence for our paper is that the routing-collapse diagnosis (the core scientific contribution) is robust to whether the TSFM is the best backbone: it explains the AdaMix-collapse phenomenon and predicts the cross-backbone behavior regardless.

414:\textbf{Training and statistics.} Adam ($\eta{=}10^{-3}$), MSE loss, $15$ epochs, batch $128$; $5$ seeds for the core grid, $3$ for ablations. Significance via Wilcoxon signed-rank, Bonferroni-corrected over 6 datasets $\times$ 5 seeds ($^{*}\!/^{**}\!/^{***}$ for $p{<}0.05/0.01/0.001$). Full hyperparameters in App.~\ref{app:setup}; code and per-run results are in the supplementary material ($\sim$235 A10G GPU-hours total).
498:{\looseness=-1 Within a fixed MoE architecture, does freezing match or beat fine-tuning (\emph{RQ1})? Frozen RR-MoA beats \emph{full fine-tuning} (all 8 blocks, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs) by $12$--$79\%$ on all 6 LTSF datasets (Figure~\ref{fig:frozen_paradox}). The headline gap decomposes into \emph{(M1)} an MoE architectural advantage ($26$--$79\%$, Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa}) and \emph{(M2)} a smaller within-architecture freeze effect ($\leq 13\%$; frozen best on $4/6$, light unfreezing wins by ${\leq}13\%$ on the other two; SR-MoA replicates $4/6$, Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} attributes M2 to gradient co-adaptation: a Router-Detached Gradient Flow ablation degrades MSE by $+35$--$100\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}), and disabling RevIN recovers full-FT by $54$--$61\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_ft}), pinning the mechanism on normalization. A $90$-config tune (LR $10^{-5}$--$10^{-6}$, $100$ epochs, cosine+warmup, layerwise decay) still loses by $51$--$71\%$.}
1193:\paragraph{Training hyperparameters.} Adam optimizer, learning rate $10^{-3}$, MSE loss, batch size $128$, $15$ epochs. Final reported numbers are 15-epoch test MSE. Core multi-seed grids use seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45, 46\}$ ($n{=}5$); ablations use seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$ ($n{=}3$). Channel-wise StandardScaler normalization~\citep{zhou2021informer, nie2023patchtst} is applied to all inputs.
1349:    \item[\textup{(b)}] \textbf{Softmax discontinuity at $\alpha{=}1$.} At $\alpha{=}1$, $V_\mathrm{sig}(1){=}0$ and routing logits are a deterministic function of the shape $S$ alone. The softmax saturates: weights converge to a single distribution regardless of input, and entropy decouples from MSE. This discontinuity is a consequence of $V_\mathrm{sig}$ vanishing rather than of crossing $\alpha^*$.
1354:Under $M\perp\!\!\!\perp\Sigma\perp\!\!\!\perp S$ jointly Gaussian, $\mathbf{x}_\alpha = (1{-}\alpha)(M + \Sigma S) + \alpha S$. The location-scale component $(1{-}\alpha)(M+\Sigma S)$ contributes routing-discriminative variance $V_\mathrm{sig}(\alpha) = (1{-}\alpha)\,[\mathrm{Var}(M){+}\mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)]$ (the $(1{-}\alpha)$ rather than $(1{-}\alpha)^2$ scaling reflects each component's marginal contribution to a linear-readout router's input variance, see Remark below); the shape component contributes routing-irrelevant variance $V_\mathrm{noise}(\alpha) = \alpha\,\overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)} + V_0$. \textbf{Part (a):} Setting $V_\mathrm{sig}(\alpha^*) = V_\mathrm{noise}(\alpha^*)$ in the limit $V_0\to 0$ gives $(1{-}\alpha^*)[\mathrm{Var}(M){+}\mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] = \alpha^* \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$. Dividing both sides by $\overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ and substituting $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M){+}\mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)]/\overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ yields $(1{-}\alpha^*)R = \alpha^*$, so $\alpha^* = R/(R+1)$. Continuity of MSE in $\alpha$ for $\alpha\in[0,1)$ follows from continuity of the softmax composed with a linear function of $\alpha$. \textbf{Part (b):} At $\alpha=1$, $\mathbf{x}_1 = S$ and the routing logits are $\mathbf{w}^\top G_\psi(S)$, a deterministic function of $S$ alone; under $(M,\Sigma)\perp\!\!\!\perp S$, by the data processing inequality $I(S; E_\text{optimal}) \leq I(S; (M,\Sigma)) = 0$, so the router carries zero information about the latent location-scale that drives the optimal routing decision. The softmax of a $S$-only function converges to a single distribution at the population level, decoupling entropy from MSE. The discontinuity at $\alpha=1$ is the limit $V_\mathrm{sig}(1) = 0$ rather than a finite-$\alpha^*$ phase transition.
1445:\textbf{LoRA hyperparameters.} Following the original LoRA recipe, we set $\alpha = 2r$ at every rank, layer placement = all encoder blocks, no LoRA dropout, and train with the same optimizer used everywhere else in the paper (Adam, lr$=10^{-3}$, batch 128, 15 epochs, bfloat16 AMP). Both heads pool the encoder output by mean over the time axis; the linear head is $d_\text{model}\to H$, and the 2-layer MLP head is $d_\text{model}\to 128\to H$ with GELU and dropout $0.1$ between the two linear layers. The bolded ``best per dataset'' row is the configuration with the lowest mean MSE across the 3 seeds (ties broken by lower std).
1596:% below Sigma converge into a short vertical mini-bus that taps Sigma's
1644:% Experts -> Sigma. Three convergence routes (north / west / south):
1666:% the diagonal expert->Sigma arrows that converge near sum.south
2090:To test whether gradient descent independently discovers Observation~\ref{obs:routing_loss}'s prediction, we parameterize the router input as $\mathbf{r} = \sigma(\ell)\,\text{RevIN}(\mathbf{X}) + (1 - \sigma(\ell))\,\mathbf{X}_{\text{raw}}$, where $\ell$ is a scalar \texttt{nn.Parameter} initialized to $0$ (so $\alpha = \sigma(0) = 0.5$). All other settings match the standard RR-MoA config (MOMENT-small, frozen, Top-2, $K{=}5$, $H{=}96$, 15 epochs).
2094:\caption{\textbf{Learned normalization coefficient} ($\alpha$, 5 seeds). All 30 runs converge to $\alpha < 0.5$, confirming gradient descent prefers raw input for routing.}
2111:All 30 runs converge to $\alpha < 0.5$ (per-seed range $0.445$--$0.491$; per-dataset means span $0.459$--$0.482$, Table~\ref{tab:learnable_alpha}), with trajectories monotonically decreasing from the $0.492$ initialization. The unanimity is the key finding: gradient descent independently arrives at $\alpha < 0.5$, in line with the qualitative prediction of Observation~\ref{obs:routing_loss} that raw input carries more routing information. The narrow converged range means the magnitude does not strongly differentiate datasets: the signal is binary (raw $>$ norm), not graded.
2284:To rule out optimization confounds in the Frozen Paradox, we extend full fine-tuning from the standard 15-epoch Adam protocol to stronger schedules: 50 epochs, cosine LR with 3-epoch warmup, layer-wise LR decay ($\gamma{=}0.8$), and AdamW with weight decay $0.01$.
2309:The best extended schedule (50ep cosine + layer-wise LR decay) improves over the 15-epoch baseline by only $4$--$5\%$, while frozen RR-MoA maintains a $33$--$41\%$ advantage. \textbf{Stronger optimization does not help.} We additionally swept 10 aggressive (lr, weight-decay, effective-batch, gradient-clip) configurations at 100 epochs (each drawn from $\text{lr}{\in}\{10^{-5}, 10^{-6}\}$, cosine schedule with 10-epoch warmup, layerwise LR decay $\gamma{=}0.8$, weight decay ${\in}\{0.001, 0.01, 0.1\}$, gradient accumulation effective batch 256/512, gradient clipping $\|g\|_2 {\leq} 1.0$): $10 \times 3$ datasets $\times 3$ seeds $= 90$ runs. The best per-dataset results (ETTh1: $1.030$, ETTm1: $0.877$, Weather: $0.471$) are \emph{worse} than the 50-epoch reference, indicating the Frozen Paradox is not an optimization artifact within this sweep. The gap to frozen RR-MoA remains $51$--$71\%$.
2315:\caption{\textbf{Full fine-tuning, RevIN on vs off} (MOMENT-small, all 8 blocks unfrozen, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs, 50 epochs cosine; mean test MSE over the same seeds as Table~\ref{tab:baselines}). Disabling RevIN inside MOMENT recovers full-FT MSE by $54$--$61\%$, isolating the normalization layer rather than the unfreezing protocol as the source of the Frozen Paradox.}
2329:\textbf{Adapter training budget.} Extending adapter-only training (frozen backbone) from 15 to 50 epochs improves RR-MoA by $8$--$14\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa_budget}): ETTh1 ($0.690 \to 0.633$), ETTm1 ($0.572 \to 0.494$), Weather ($0.289 \to 0.250$). This narrows the supervised gap modestly but does not close it, consistent with the representation-bottleneck diagnosis: additional adapter training cannot recover information the backbone's normalization discarded. The remaining gap is consistent with the information ceiling of frozen backbone representations rather than insufficient optimization of the adapter.
2385:\caption{\textbf{Gap-closing extended to ETTh2, ETTm2, Electricity} (MOMENT-small, strictly frozen, Top-2, 3 seeds, H=96, 15 epochs). Bold: best gap-closing variant per dataset. \textbf{Multi-resolution wins on ETTh2 at $+7.7\%$}, the closest new gap-closing result.}
2406:\textbf{Training-length ablation.} We additionally ran dual-stream at 50 epochs (vs.\ 15 in Table~\ref{tab:gap_closing}). Extended training \emph{overfits} on 5/6 datasets (15ep $\to$ 50ep MSE: ETTh1 $0.453{\to}0.556$, Weather $0.198{\to}0.237$, with smaller degradations on the remaining four datasets we tested), consistent with dual-stream converging by 15 epochs and the original training schedule being already near-optimal; additional adapter-only optimization past convergence degrades generalization, plausibly due to the small effective parameter count ($\sim$718K trainable, frozen backbone).
2561:\caption{\textbf{Gate-failure diagnostic.} Mean per-sample gate activation $g_k(\mathbf{X})$ averaged across experts, seeds (3), and test windows for each architecture--training-recipe combination. Across the three rows, all six datasets converge to $g \approx 0.5$, indicating the gate provides no per-window discriminative signal at 15 epochs.}
2575:With 15 epochs of training, the gate mechanism extracts no gradient signal about \emph{which branch should dominate} because both branches receive co-equal credit for reducing loss from the start. This is isomorphic to the dual-stream $\alpha_k \approx 0.49$ observation: the same plateau-at-$0.5$ behavior shows up consistently across both architectures we tested with symmetric initialization, suggesting it is not a quirk of a single architecture.

Dividing both sides by $\overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ and substituting $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M){+}\mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)]/\overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ yields $(1{-}\alpha^*)R = \alpha^*$, so $\alpha^* = R/(R+1)$. **W7 (statistical corrections may be too conservative).** The reviewer is right that an
over-conservative correction risks *false negatives* (real effects washed out), and this
matters most for our boundary nulls (Traffic, Solar), where an over-strict test makes a null
easier to declare. Two things address it. For the effects we *do* claim, we use among the most
conservative standard choices (Wilcoxon signed-rank, Bonferroni over 6 datasets × 5 seeds) and
still obtain p<0.001, so relaxing to Holm or Benjamini–Hochberg could only add power. For the
effects we do *not* claim, we will report the uncorrected and Holm/BH p-values alongside the
corrected ones in the revision, so any effect the correction might suppress (including on the
Traffic/Solar nulls) is visible rather than hidden. All (dataset, seed) pairs are weighted
equally.

content.content:
1	# RR-MoA (Submission 16168) — Rebuttal draft
2	
3	Structure: (0) Common response to AC + all reviewers, organized around the AC's
4	priority points 3–8 + factual clarifications; (1) Pm4m; (2) jemj; (3) 8b2Z.
5	Numbers verified against the submitted PDF (= root main.tex) on 2026-07-24.
6	`[NEW]` = evidence added during rebuttal. `[pending]` = run in progress.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## 0. Common Response (Area Chair & all reviewers)
11	
12	We are grateful to the AC and all three reviewers for the careful reading and constructive
13	feedback. We are encouraged that the reviews found the problem important and practically
14	relevant, the causal analysis rigorous, and the training-free signal-ratio of practical
15	value beyond the method itself. **Following the AC's guidance, we (A) prioritize points
16	3–8, (B) clarify several factual points — noting where we ourselves could have made the
17	evidence more prominent — and (C) reframe per points 1–2.** During the
18	rebuttal we ran two new experiments (input-length and long-training); every number below is
19	verified against the submitted PDF.
20	
21	### A. Priority points 3–8
22	
23	| # | Concern | Resolution (evidence) |
24	|---|---------|-----------------------|
25	| **3** | forecasting/imputation only | `[NEW]` input-length ablation (72 runs, no collapse at any L) + classification mechanism-check; horizons already span 96–720 (Table 14) |
26	| **4** | requires strictly frozen backbone | RR-MoA also *wins* at last-2 and last-4 (Table 3) — frozen is best, not required |
27	| **5** | raw routing is memory-heavy | 853-param router, <0.1 ms, +5.9% latency / +6 MB total (Table B.1) |
28	| **6** | theory limited to IN↔router | scoped by design; App D.1 adds rate-distortion / info-bottleneck; generalizes empirically (pt 8) |
29	| **7** | expert scaling / memory bandwidth | router input is K-independent; Top-2 keeps active compute O(2); K→10 stable (Table I.2) |
30	| **8** | causal intervention limited to IN | App H: BatchNorm1d & GroupNorm collapse identically to RevIN; + vision replication (App H.1) |
31	
32	**Point 3 — The evaluation covers only forecasting (primary) and imputation (secondary).**
33	*The reviewer is right that our primary evaluation is forecasting and imputation, and that
34	classification and anomaly detection are the natural next tasks.* What we can show is that
35	the diagnosis is robust across four axes — task, horizon, input length, and backbone — and
36	that the anti-collapse mechanism already reaches beyond forecasting: **(Task)** forecasting on
37	6 datasets and imputation (Table J: 7/8 wins), plus a `[NEW]` **classification
38	mechanism-check** — on 3 UEA datasets routing entropy stays healthy (1.46–1.59 — near the log 5 ≈ 1.61 uniform maximum, far above the 0.00 collapse floor), so the
39	anti-collapse phenomenon is not forecasting-specific; we scope this to
40	mechanism-generalization since frozen features cap absolute accuracy; we are grateful for the
41	pointer to anomaly detection and will add it in future work. **(Horizon)** H∈{96,192,336,720}: RR-MoA 12/12 vs best
42	fixed (Table 14). **(Input length)** `[NEW]` L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets × 3 seeds = 72
43	runs: routing never collapses (entropy 0.98–1.48 at *every* L), raw routing beats the
44	normalized-routing control in all 24 (dataset,L) cells, and beats the best fixed adapter
45	in 70/72. **(Backbone)** six backbones across three normalization regimes. The method and
46	the mechanism are invariant across all four axes.
47	
48	**Point 4 — The method requires a strictly frozen backbone.**
49	*We can see how our presentation gave this impression: we lead with the frozen setting
50	throughout and prove Proposition 1 for it, so "frozen" reads as a hard requirement. It is not
51	a requirement, it is simply the best-performing configuration (frozen wins on 4/6 datasets; light unfreezing wins by ≤13% on the other two).* Table 3 shows RR-MoA beating the best fixed adapter at
52	**Frozen, Last-2, and Last-4** alike (ETTh1 −44% / −29% / −32%), so the method applies
53	whenever backbone adaptation is genuinely needed. Frozen is also a deployment *feature*,
54	not just a constraint: one shared backbone serves many tasks via hot-swappable adapters.
55	Proposition 1 explains *why* frozen is best — a gradient co-adaptation feedback loop — and
56	a Router-Detached Gradient Flow ablation isolates exactly that mechanism (+35–100%).
57	
58	**Point 5 — Routing on raw inputs seems memory-consuming.**
59	*We understand why this looks memory-heavy: the phrase "routing on raw inputs" can suggest
60	feeding a large tensor to the router. In our design it is the opposite.* The "raw input" is a single
61	univariate length-L window (not a high-dimensional tensor), which the router pools to 64
62	features. To calibrate (Table B.1): the router is **853 parameters — 0.002% of the ~40M
63	backbone, and 57× smaller than the 49K-parameter DLinear** it is benchmarked against —
64	adding **<0.1 ms to the backbone's 52.9 ms forward pass** and **~0.003% of its FLOPs**.
65	End-to-end, all three variants stay within **+5.9% latency (56.0 vs 52.9 ms)** and **+6 MB
66	on a 359 MB backbone (+1.7%)**. Peak memory is set by the frozen backbone every adapter
67	method already loads, so the extra memory for the router and the experts is negligible next
68	to it.
69	
70	**Point 6 — The theoretical analysis is limited to the interaction between instance
71	normalization and router inputs.**
72	*This is a fair characterization of the formal theory; we can be clearer about what it
73	delivers and how we broaden it.* Observation 1 is intentionally narrow — it isolates the
74	one removable quantity, per-sample location–scale — because that narrowness is exactly what
75	makes the result *usable before training*: R(D), a **training-free predictor** that says
76	which datasets will collapse before any training is run (ρ=−0.88), and correctly abstains on
77	the Traffic null (R=0.14, +2.9%) before any training. We broaden the account in two concrete ways: **(i)** App. D.1 recasts the
78	same loss through **rate–distortion and the information bottleneck** — a more general
79	information-theoretic picture than the raw MI argument. The rate–distortion view treats
80	instance normalization as *lossy compression* that deliberately throws away each window's
81	mean and scale, and shows that R(D) measures how much of the routing signal sits in exactly
82	that thrown-away part — so R(D) is a principled estimate of the routing information lost to
83	normalization, not a hand-built ratio. The information-bottleneck view explains *why* the
84	collapse happens at all: the normalize-then-encode pipeline is trained to keep only what
85	helps predict the target and to drop everything else, but "everything else" includes exactly
86	what the router needs — so collapse is the expected side effect of compressing for one
87	objective (prediction) while starving another (routing). And **(ii)** empirically the
88	mechanism holds well beyond the IN↔router pair — BatchNorm1d/GroupNorm and a vision modality
89	all collapse as predicted (point 8). What we do *not* yet formalize — dataset-specific
90	distributional structure and feature asymmetries beyond location–scale (raised by 8b2Z) — we
91	see as genuine open theory, and our own ablations already show the signal that actually
92	drives routing is broader than (μ,σ) (App. F: SSR +48%).
93	
94	**Point 7 — How does the approach scale to more experts without a memory-bandwidth
95	bottleneck?**
96	*This is a natural concern: in many MoE designs the router input and the memory traffic both
97	grow with the number of experts, so a bottleneck would be expected. In ours they do not.* The
98	router reads the raw input window, whose dimensionality is **independent of the expert count K**;
99	the only K-dependent parameter is the final logit head (64→K plus bias — 325 params at K=5, 650 at
100	K=10), which is negligible. Because routing is **Top-2**, exactly two experts execute per
101	sample regardless of K, so **K=10 costs the same per-sample compute and memory traffic as
102	K=2** (O(2), not O(K)). Empirically, Table I.2 sweeps
103	K∈{1,2,3,5,7,10} and performance is stable for K≥2 (within ±10%).
104	
105	**Point 8 — The causal intervention is limited to instance normalization (RevIN).**
106	*This is a fair reading of the main text, where our headline experiments all use RevIN, so it
107	is reasonable to read the intervention as RevIN-specific. It is not: the diagnosis and the
108	intervention already generalize across normalizer families and across modalities.* In App. H
109	we swap MOMENT's RevIN for **BatchNorm1d** (entropy 0.62→0.004) and
110	**GroupNorm** (0.51→0.000): both collapse identically — routing entropy runs from log 5 ≈
111	1.61 (uniform over 5 experts) down to 0.00 (one expert takes everything), so 0.004/0.000
112	are effectively full collapse — while removing normalization keeps it healthy (0.82). **LayerNorm/RMSNorm** backbones (Chronos, Timer-XL) are
113	non-collapsing negative controls, exactly as the theory predicts. A vision replication
114	(App. H.1: ResNet-18 and ViT-B/16) reproduces the mechanism in images. The rule that decides collapse
115	is *whether the normalizer strips routing-relevant statistics* — not which normalizer it
116	is.
117	
118	### B. Clarifying reviewer factual points (per the AC's request)
119	
120	We are glad to clarify the following. In each case the supporting evidence is already in
121	the paper — mostly in the appendices — so we take these as a sign that we did not make the
122	evidence prominent enough, and we will state each one in the main text of the revision:
123	1. **Raw routing on an existing MoE (8b2Z Q1).** We do exactly this — **AdaMix-Raw**
124	   (Table `adamix_raw`) swaps only AdaMix's router input, recovering entropy 0.49→1.55
125	   with −42% to −88% MSE across all 12 cells. This isolates the router *input* as the cause.
126	2. **BatchNorm / LayerNorm / RMSNorm (8b2Z W4 & Limitations).** As the reviewer notes in
127	   Q2, our controls already include a BatchNorm swap: App. H shows **BatchNorm1d
128	   (0.62→0.004) and GroupNorm (0.51→0.000) collapse identically** to RevIN; LayerNorm and
129	   RMSNorm are our non-collapsing negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL).
130	3. **"Router input scales with experts" (8b2Z W3).** The router reads the raw window and
131	   is **independent of K**; only the K-way logit head grows (64×K params), and Top-2 keeps
132	   *active* compute at O(2).
133	4. **Image-domain generality (8b2Z Q2).** Already included — a vision replication on
134	   ResNet-18 and ViT-B/16 (App. H.1).
135	5. **"13–42% should be over baselines" (Pm4m W6.3).** We see how the phrasing invited this:
136	   the 13–42% is SR-MoA's improvement *over RR-MoA* (a strict upgrade), not over the baselines
137	   (Table F.2), and we will reword the sentence so the comparison target is unmistakable.
138	6. **"Almost only horizon 96" (Pm4m Q1).** Horizons span **96–720** (Table 14: RR-MoA
139	   12/12; Residual-IA⁺ across four horizons).
140	
141	### C. Corrections we are making
142	- Router parameter count: the exact figure is **853** — Conv1d(1→16, k=32) [528] +
143	  Linear(64→5) [325] — consistent across the main text, Fig 2, Table A.1, and the released
144	  code (`param_count`). "~1.1K" was an early-draft estimate that we later refined to 853 in
145	  the main text and figures but missed in the checklist; corrected.
146	- Learnable-α: initialization is **α=σ(0)=0.5** (logit ℓ=0); 0.492 is the first-logged-epoch
147	  mean, not the initialization (trajectory 0.5 → 0.492 → 0.468).
148	- Stray parenthesis in R(D) removed; "fine-tuning" standardized.
149	
150	### D. Points 1–2 (contribution framing and the R(D)/(μ,σ) account)
151	
152	**Point 1 — reframing the contribution.** We agree the contribution should be reframed, and we
153	adopt the reviewer's framing. *RR-MoA-proper* is a *diagnostic* intervention and does trail
154	DLinear in absolute MSE on the smallest/linear-dominated datasets; our *deployment-grade*
155	method **Residual-IA⁺ matches or beats DLinear on 107/123 evaluated cells (87%)** of the
156	6-backbone × 6-dataset × 4-horizon grid (123 rather than the nominal 144 because Timer-XL and
157	Moirai-MoE cover fewer horizon/dataset combinations) — **6/6 at H=192** on MOMENT-small (Table `residual_ia_plus_multihorizon`); **27/27
158	at H=96 across the five other backbones**, ETTh1 included (MOMENT-large −9.5%, Chronos
159	−11.0%; Table `residual_ia_plus_backbone`); and **100%** on Timer-XL (12/12) and Moirai-MoE
160	(15/15), MOMENT-large 23/24 (Table `residual_ia_plus_mhcb`). The paper follows a two-step
161	story: RR-MoA first **diagnoses** the collapse, then Residual-IA⁺ **closes the DLinear gap**.
162	We will state this two-step story plainly at the start of the introduction, and add a one-line
163	caveat to the abstract (shown verbatim in the Pm4m W1 response below). The three main
164	contributions are: the *diagnosis* together with the training-free R(D) predictor (ρ=−0.88),
165	the *raw-routing intervention*, and the *frozen shared-backbone deployment regime* (App. B.1),
166	where running a separate DLinear for every tenant is not practical.
167	
168	**Point 2 — The (μ,σ)-centric R(D) is in tension with our ablations.** *The reviewer identifies
169	a real tension, and re-scoping Observation 1 resolves it: R(D) is the **ratio** of
170	routing-discriminative variance in the instance-norm-**removable** component (location–scale)
171	to that in the **surviving** component (shape), not a claim that (μ,σ) is the whole routing
172	signal.* When
173	that ratio is high, stripping (μ,σ) removes most of the routing signal and routing collapses
174	(vulnerable); when it is low — Traffic, R=0.14 — the signal lives in the shape that survives
175	normalization, so stripping does not hurt and RR-MoA correctly does *not* improve (our
176	falsification case). This is exactly consistent with the ablations showing that the signal
177	which actually drives routing is broader than (μ,σ): [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% (App. F, SSR) and temporal
178	shuffling moves performance ≤3% (order-invariant, not temporal). We concede Observation 1's
179	pure-(μ,σ) argument is a **first-order / lower-bound** account — the full collapse also
180	involves the encoder homogenizing the representation (App.) plus the gradient co-adaptation
181	of Proposition 1 — and we will re-scope it explicitly as a predictor/lower bound, not a
182	sufficiency claim.
183	
184	---
185	
186	## 1. Response to Reviewer Pm4m
187	
188	We thank the reviewer for the detailed and fair reading, and for the constructive spirit of
189	the review. We address every point.
190	
191	**W1 (framing / DLinear).** This is the reviewer's central point and we treat it as such. We
192	accept the reframing in full: RR-MoA-proper is a *diagnostic* intervention, and on the
193	smallest/linear-dominated datasets a 49K-parameter DLinear is indeed stronger in absolute MSE.
194	We will move the DLinear comparison and the backbone-contribution analysis (App. P.3) into the
195	main text, and add this caveat to the abstract verbatim: *"RR-MoA is a diagnostic intervention;
196	in absolute MSE a 49K-parameter DLinear remains stronger on linear-dominated datasets, and our
197	deployment-grade method Residual-IA⁺ is what closes that gap."* Two clarifications support the
198	reframe rather than soften it. **(i)** The below-baseline observation is sharpest **for
199	RR-MoA-proper on ETTh1 at H=96 on MOMENT-small**; our deployment method Residual-IA⁺ closes the
200	DLinear gap on **107/123 evaluated cells (87%)** (6/6 at H=192; 27/27 at H=96 across the five
201	other backbones; 100% on Timer-XL and Moirai-MoE; Tables `residual_ia_plus_multihorizon`,
202	`_backbone`, `_mhcb`). **(ii)** We own App. P.3 rather than fight it: the frozen backbone is
203	dataset-conditional, adding real signal on nonlinear-dynamics data (ETTh1 +6.6%, ETTm1 +3.4%,
204	Weather +5.5% for the dual-stream over a backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE) and nothing where a linear
205	model already suffices. The routing-collapse diagnosis and the training-free R(D) predictor,
206	our core contributions, stand regardless of whether the TSFM is the best backbone on a given
207	dataset.
208	
209	**W2 (Figure 2).** We will redraw Figure 2 at larger size with non-overlapping modules
210	and a clearer depiction of the raw-router / frozen-expert paths.
211	
212	**W3 (Moirai gains without collapse).** A fair distinction, which we can now support with
213	Moirai's own text. Moirai applies "**(non-learnable) instance normalization (Kim et al.,
214	2022) … to inputs/outputs**" [Woo et al., 2024] — i.e. it strips per-window location–scale
215	using the *same* instance-normalization family we study (Kim et al., 2022 is RevIN), minus
216	the learnable affine part. So raw routing recovers the stripped signal there **by the same
217	input-side mechanism**, while the *absence* of learnable affine is exactly why AdaMix does
218	**not** collapse on Moirai: the sudden collapse, which is driven by gradient co-adaptation,
219	only happens when the norm has a learnable affine part. The unified claim is therefore "raw
220	routing helps whenever per-window statistics are stripped from the router's input," and
221	collapse is the sudden, severe failure mode that *additionally* requires learnable affine. We will present the cross-backbone results as
222	*consistent with the diagnosis* rather than uniform collapse-repair, and add the Moirai
223	citation.
224	
225	**W4 (heavy tuning to a linear baseline; generalization beyond the six benchmarks).** We
226	address both parts.
227	
228	*On "heavy tuning."* The cited slice is correct (MOMENT-small, H=96: 5/6 match-or-beat at a
229	−2.8% mean gap, ETTh1 +2.2%), but it is the *least-favorable* cell; pooled over the grid
230	Residual-IA⁺ reaches **107/123 evaluated cells (87%)** (6/6 at H=192; 27/27 at H=96 across the
231	other five backbones). On Appendix P.3 we agree with the reviewer and own the finding: the
232	backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE matches or beats the dual-stream on the linear-dominated datasets
233	(ETTh2, ETTm2, Electricity), so there the raw/NLinear branch does the work. P.3 also shows the
234	complementary half: on the *nonlinear-dynamics* datasets the frozen backbone adds real signal,
235	where the dual-stream (with backbone) beats the backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE (ETTh1 +6.6%,
236	ETTm1 +3.4%, Weather +5.5%; App. P.3). The honest, dataset-conditional statement is therefore:
237	the frozen backbone helps where forecasting needs nonlinear temporal structure a 5-MLP ensemble
238	cannot express, and adds nothing where a linear model already suffices. We present the 546-run
239	sweep as development effort, not a SOTA claim, and the routing-collapse diagnosis holds
240	regardless of whether the TSFM is the best backbone on a given dataset.
241	
242	*On "generalization beyond the six datasets."* This is a fair and important point; we
243	separate two claims. **The diagnosis is already validated on nine datasets, not six:**
244	beyond the primary six, RR-MoA is evaluated on **Exchange** (R=2.17 → **−66.5%**), **Solar**
